In the first study, Ding et al. [60] used ML algorithms to predict elastic modulus (E), tensile strength (σmax), and elongation at break (ɛr) of polyurethane elastomers. The dataset was compiled through data mining from academic literature and refined using recursive data elimination, which helped to remove noise and inconsistencies to improve data quality. Among the five tested models, XGB achieved the highest predictive accuracy across all three target properties [60].

Another study employed a deep neural network (DNN), improved by Bayesian optimization, to predict E, σmax, and Poisson’s ratio (ν) from nanoindentation load–depth curves of polycarbonate (PC) and polymethyl methacrylate. The dataset, generated via finite element simulations, was used to train the DNN architecture comprising two hidden layers with exponential linear unit activation function, and optimizers such as adaptive moment estimation function (Adam) and stochastic gradient descent. Bayesian optimization was applied to minimize the MAE during training, resulting in a model with R2 values of 0.99 or higher for all predicted properties. Experimental validation showed that the prediction results were close to the literature results [61].

Similarly, the influence of nano-TiO₂ and cellulose nanocrystals on fracture strength, yield strength, and Young’s modulus in high-density polyethylene nanobiocomposites was investigated through a multifaceted methodological framework. This included the application of analysis of variance to determine statistically significant factors, response surface methodology for constructing predictive statistical models, and an artificial neural network coupled with genetic algorithm (ANN-GA) hybrid model for optimization purposes. The experimental dataset was derived from specimens fabricated via injection molding and subsequently subjected to mechanical testing protocols. The ANN model demonstrated high predictive accuracy for the target mechanical properties, while the ANN-GA approach effectively mitigated overfitting risks and facilitated model-driven optimization of formulation parameters [62].

In addition to mechanical analysis, thermal property prediction has become a growing area of interest in polymer research using ML. Malashin et al. [32] applied 11 ML models to predict polymer properties, including glass transition temperature (Tg), thermal decomposition temperature (Tad), melting temperature (Tm), and crystallization kinetics (k). The dataset was extracted from the PolYinfo database [63], and was used to train the algorithms according to the tested property. Before training, molecular features were derived from SMILES representations. Among the tested models, random forest, XGBoost, and gradient boosting showed the strongest performance, particularly with larger datasets, while bagging, K neighbor regressor, and SVR were more effective for smaller sample sizes.

Researchers predicted the Tg of poly(meth)acrylates, including polymers with phenyl rings, using RvNN. Two molecular representation approaches were explored: group representation, treating cyclic groups as single units, and cycle breaking representation using standard formats like Unique SMILES. The dataset containing 217 training samples and 54 test samples yielded an R2 of 0.9351 using the recursive cascade correlation recurrent neural network (RNN) with InChI representation [45].

Finally, researchers introduced a deep learning approach that leverages CNN with fully connected layers to predict the glass transition temperature (Tg) directly from monomeric chemical structures. In this method, SMILES strings were transformed into binary images and passed through a CNN architecture comprising two convolutional layers with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function, max-pooling, and dropout rates between 20% and 30%. The model was evaluated on both a restricted dataset (~100 polymers) and a larger dataset (>200 polymers), achieving prediction errors below 6% [42].

In summary, the reviewed studies consistently demonstrate that machine learning-based approaches can significantly lower experimental costs while improving the accuracy of physicochemical property predictions.

2.2.4 Language-based and predictive platforms

Limitations in polymer data previously delayed their application, but advancements in data standardization and augmentation now enable breakthroughs. Language models excel at addressing multimodal and multidomain challenges, making them ideal for understanding the complex relationships between polymer compositions as also their properties.

PolyNC, developed by researchers is an advanced natural/chemical language model designed to predict polymeric properties with high accuracy and efficiency. By using advanced data augmentation and tokenization strategies and by integrating natural and SMILES chemical languages, it operates as an end-to-end solution for multitask learning, reducing data preprocessing and enhancing generalization for polymer discovery and property prediction [36].

Another language-based model is TransPolymer. Instead of relying solely on conventional machine learning techniques, it employs masked language model to pretrain approximately 5 million unlabeled polymers, followed by fine-tuning. The predictive performance of the model was tested against 10 conventional machine learning algorithms across multiple properties and outperformed the traditional algorithms [63].

Polymer Genome (available at polymergenome.org) is a practical, easy-to-use platform that uses supervised machine learning models to predict polymer properties from chemical structure and composition. A dataset containing both computationally derived and experimentally measured polymer properties is used. To improve property predictions, the platform uses a hierarchical fingerprinting scheme that captures structural features from atomic-level connectivity to morphological characteristics, using GPR, ensuring accurate predictions with uncertainty quantification. The online platform enables users to input polymer structures via SMILES strings or an interactive molecular sketch tool, allowing for rapid on-demand property predictions [64].

2.3 Molecular structure design and automated polymer synthesis using machine learning

For many years, the study of structure–property relationships in macromolecular materials, including block copolymers, polymer blends, and polymer nanocomposites, has been central to polymer science and engineering. Research has shown that, beyond choosing the polymer chemistry and architecture, the final material properties are determined by the assembled structures, which are often hierarchical and span multiple scales. Due to the recent breakthroughs in polymer synthesis/processing technologies, the range of achievable equilibrated and non-equilibrated structures has expanded significantly. Identifying the optimal structures that produce the desired properties, while minimizing costs and efforts for industrial-scale production, is a key driver for high-throughput experimentation. The rising demand for high-throughput experiments also creates a greater need for rapid, and ideally automated, analysis of synthesized materials and their characterization, highlighting the importance of developing appropriate ML workflows [65].

The molecular architecture of polymers is fundamentally based on macromolecules that are either synthesized through chemical processes or derived from natural sources. A critical feature of both natural and synthetic polymers is the capacity of carbon atoms to form extensive molecular chains. Polymers are constructed from fundamental repeating units known as monomers. In synthetic polymerization processes, monomers are covalently bonded to form molecular chains through mechanisms such as addition polymerization or condensation polymerization. These macromolecules can exhibit either linear or branched configurations. Typically, a single macromolecule consists of several hundred monomers linked together [66].

An essential determinant of a polymer’s physical properties is the spatial arrangement of its molecular chains, which is helpful in the material’s processability and suitability for molding. This arrangement is divided into two distinct categories: physical and chemical configurations. Chemical arrangements are characterized by irreversible cross-linking of molecular chains, where covalent bonds form a permanent three-dimensional network. In contrast, physical arrangements are reversible, involving merely entangled chains without the formation of permanent chemical bonds [67].

In the context of new material design, various techniques assist researchers in pushing the limits of polymer design. One such method is the use of robust design of experiments (DoE) approaches, which are essential for methodically exploring the design space and achieving the desired properties of materials. This process often requires decisions to be made across several areas, such as material properties, operational conditions, and system configurations. Conventional design methodologies, which often rely on experience-based approaches, present numerous challenges that can hinder the optimization and reliability of the material design process [68].

The reduction in the number of experiments (and associated costs) and the exploratory nature of DoE have had significant impact in the field of architecture. However, DoE typically relies on a range of conditions within which the mathematical models are valid and provide satisfactory predictions. Conditions outside the selected range may reduce the accuracy of the mathematical models, causing the experimental response to differ significantly from the predicted response [69].

ML regression algorithms, in conjunction with feature engineering and extensive datasets, are instrumental in predicting material properties for advanced fabrication and practical applications. By leveraging available data for training, researchers can markedly reduce the time and costs traditionally required for experimental procedures. These algorithms are helpful in the optimization and discovery of functional materials across a range of disciplines, including thermoelectric, photovoltaics, catalysis, and optics [70].

A notable limitation of existing algorithms is the insufficient availability of data, which hinders the development of AI/ML-based algorithms for predicting the behavior of polymer materials. Machine learning algorithms rely on large datasets for training and improving their predictive accuracy. In the absence of comprehensive data, these models are unable to generate reliable predictions of polymer behavior across varied scenarios, thereby complicating the development of robust, ML-driven materials for polymer development [71]. However, where conventional physical and chemical models exhibit limitations, ML models are increasingly addressing these gaps with remarkable speed and precision.

The integration of these approaches has been referred to in multiple ways (such as self-driving laboratory, autonomous platform, or closed-loop experiments), but the common result is a faster pace of discovery and a deeper understanding of highly refined materials [72].

2.4 Polymer characterization through computer vision and spectrum analysis

Polymers are increasingly being used in various areas of knowledge. Therefore, before using these materials, it is necessary to understand their characteristics and applications. For this, several analyses are carried out in order to identify polymeric properties (e.g., hardness, impact resistance, and tensile strength). The main spectral analyses and computer vision are described below.

2.4.1 Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR)

In this technique, an infrared light beam interacts with the polymer, inducing vibrations in the molecule’s atoms. These vibrations are linked to specific frequencies of chemical bonds, reflecting the molecule’s energy levels. They are influenced by the molecular structure, the shape of the molecule’s potential energy surface, atomic masses, and possibly, vibrational interactions [73]. One of the main advantages of using Attenuated Total Reflectance spectroscopy (ATR) is that it allows samples to be analyzed with very little or no preparation.

2.4.2 Raman spectroscopy

Raman spectroscopy is a vibrational technique that can obtain information about the structure of molecules and the nature of chemical bonds [74]. Raman scattering signals are obtained due to the excitation of the normal vibrational modes of molecules by monochromatic excitation radiation, which undergoes inelastic scattering when demonstrating changes in the polarizability of molecules [75].

2.4.3 Light scattering

Light scattering techniques are classified into elastic or dynamic and static modes. Both are employed in the characterization of polymers [76]. The almost elastic light scattering allows information about the hydrodynamic radius to be obtained, but it does not directly provide the average molar mass of the polymer [77]. For this reason, its application in polymer characterization is limited when the average molar mass is an essential parameter. However, this technique is useful to evaluate the degree of branching of polymers formed from the same monomers, since more branched polymers have a smaller hydrodynamic radius in a suitable solvent, i.e., a solvent that interacts well with polymeric chains [78].

Static laser light scattering in the so-called Debye system allows the measurement of the average molar mass (weighted by the mass) of polymers, ranging from a few tens to millions of Daltons [79].

2.4.4 Computer vision

The use of computational models based on ML is a valuable tool for optimizing processes, which makes them faster and more reliable in predicting polymeric properties. In this way, it is possible to evaluate the efficiency of different compounds in specific applications, extracting data from chemoinformatics libraries without the need to synthesize them in the laboratory [80].

To successfully apply predictive ML models in problem solving, it is critical to employ proper preprocessing and structuring techniques for datasets [81]. When combined with high-quality data sources, these approaches ensure robust and efficient models [82]. In broad terms, ML techniques are typically categorized into supervised learning and unsupervised learning, with the former being most useful in polymer science [83].

For example, one of the applications of computer vision in polymer science involves the training of overlapping and embedded chemical substructures through the unsupervised CORPUS method, a chemoinformatics tool that preserves information about the properties of the compounds contained in a training database [84].

Furthermore, this method allows efficient grouping of high-quality data based on chemical structures. In this view, chemical descriptors represent different levels of characterization of molecular structure and can be classified based on their dimensions. This classification facilitates the interpretation of molecular properties, since the 40 dimensions of the descriptors encompass a wide variety of properties, characteristics, and physicochemical phenomena. These dimensions can be organized into categories ranging from one to six dimensions.

2.5 Modeling and simulation of polymer degradation and recycling processes

The increasing environmental concerns regarding polymeric waste have prompted significant research into the degradation and recycling of polymers. Thus, ML algorithms are a powerful tool for the prediction of polymeric behavior in both regular and extreme conditions, which helps the optimization of recycling processes [85]. In this sense, this topic explores the application of ML models, particularly RNN, such as LSTM (long short-term memory) networks and reinforcement learning (RL), in modeling polymer degradation and enhancing recyclability. Furthermore, Figure 2.1 shows the amount of scientific research carried out on this topic, where the search was performed at scopus.com using the descriptors “polymer degradation” OR “polymer recycling” AND “RNN” OR “reinforcement learning.”

According to Figure 2.1, there is an observable increase in the number of published scientific research articles from 2002 to 2025. All these studies focus on polymer science, particularly the synthesis and application of stable polymers, with the assistance of machine learning (ML) algorithms. ML is primarily employed to investigate polymer degradation and recycling, highlighting the growing interest of researchers in this promising field [86, 87, 88, 89]. Consequently, the classification of ML models for polymer degradation and recycling has emerged as a hot topic. In this view, the following sections are concerned with the concepts of RNN and Reinforcement Learning and with the discussion of the application of these ML algorithms in the polymer degradation/recycling studies.

2.5.1 Applied models: RNNs and reinforcement learning

Machine learning algorithms are valuable and helpful tools for understanding complex interactions governing polymer degradation. For example, ML algorithms can effectively identify the variables (features) that result in higher influence on polymer degradation, and use the variables to perform simulations of the polymer behavior under various scenarios and conditions [90]. Moreover, this approach enables predictions of specific variables (e.g., degradation rates, weight loss, transition temperatures), which can help in the production of optimized materials [91].

In parallel, RNN, particularly LSTM, can be used for modelling the degradation processes of polymers over time by capturing time dependency within the data [92]. This approach is valuable to analyze the change in polymeric properties with respect to time, being helpful in the synthesis of biodegradable polymers. Additionally, RL-based algorithms (e.g., Q-learning and deep Q-learning) can provide enhanced predictions since they are especially designed to interpret and reproduce complex systems [93]. Thus, it is useful to simulate recycling processes and optimize them. For instance, RL can distinguish between compostable and non-compostable polymers [94]. In this way, RL significantly improves the sorting task commonly used in recycling facilities [95].

2.5.2 RNNs: the role of LSMT in polymer science

RNN is a type of ANN. However, the main difference between conventional ANN and RNN is the capability of the latter to retain information during the learning process (i.e., forward and backpropagation steps) [96, 97]. Thus, RNN is extremely useful in time series and the investigation of dynamic systems such as financial forecast tasks and polymer behavior over time [98]. Gated recurrent units (GRUs) and LSTM networks are the main RNN algorithms used in industrial applications [99, 100, 101, 102, 103]. It is worth pointing out that in polymer science and for systems with high complexity, LSMT tends to be most effective when there are long-term patterns to be learned, such as progressive degradation over months or years, and hence will be deeply discussed in this book.

LSTM networks overcome some of these challenges by the utilization of memory cells and some mechanisms that deal with the flow of information [104]. Thus, LSTM architecture can retain significant information over time and selectively forget irrelevant details. In polymer science, LSTMs have proven particularly beneficial for investigating degradation and recycling processes [105]. Thus, Figure 2.2(a and b) illustrates the typical architecture and functioning of an RNN with LSMT layers and some of the responses expected in polymer science applications.

According to Figure 2.2, RNN-LSTM, or simply LSTM, involve the feeding of data to the input layer (Five variables: pH, time, hardness, toughness, and modulus of elasticity), processing in hidden layers (one or more LSTM layers), and the generation of a response based on pattern learning from data.

The LSTM layers are mainly concerned with pattern detection that varies with time, whereas dense layers deal only with pattern recognition without considering the time dependency of input data. Thus, LSTM deals with pattern recognition and learning from time-dependent data, being well-suited for analyzing the temporal evolution of material properties such as stability, degradation, and thermal resistance, which also enables more accurate predictions and material design optimizations [106]. Thus, LSTM is used in various applications within polymer science such as predicting degradation rates, monitoring polymerization processes, optimizing recycling, and modeling mechanical performance [107]. These capabilities help design durable materials, improve product quality, enhance recycling efficiency, and tailor polymers for specific applications [108]. Moreover, LSTM facilitates real-time monitoring of polymerization processes, enabling researchers to make adjustments that improve product quality and properties [109]. Additionally, it can simulate the recyclability of various polymers by considering their degradation profiles as well as predict specific properties (tensile strength or elasticity based on historical data), which allows optimization of polymer recycling [110].

Therefore, RNN and LSTM algorithms are characterized as powerful AI tools for use in polymer science, especially for modelling and simulation of degradation and recycling processes on bench and industrial scale. Furthermore, Table 2.2 presents some scientific papers involving the use of these AI-based algorithms in polymer science.

Table 2.2:Scientific works utilizing LSTM in polymer science.

Application LSTM configuration Findings/commentary Reference

Monitoring polymerization Bidirectional LSTM Improved real-time monitoring capabilities, leading to enhanced product quality [112]

According to Table 2.2, LSTM is extremely useful in polymer science, particularly in sorting tasks (classification of compostable and non-compostable polymers and to get insight into the biodegradability of these materials), degradation profile (based on the prediction of thermal/mechanical properties) and in the recycling process. Moreover, RNNs in these reported works have been presenting high accuracy in processing data with temporal dependency, being applicable in industrial situations.

2.5.3 RL applied to polymeric material science

RL is a subarea of ML, with a focus on training based on interactions between an environment and an agent, considering the use of an award to improve algorithm performance as the learning process occurs [116]. Thus, RL makes decisions based on a given state of the system, receiving feedback in the form of a reward-and-learn pattern for optimizing the cumulative rewards over time [117]. By trial and error, the agent explores various situations in the dataset based on the outcomes obtained in previous experiences [118, 119]. In this sense, RL can identify scenarios where optimal situations are not known and should be discovered through experimentation [120]. However, to get good results in predictions, a large dataset (and computational resources) is required [121].

Based on these observations, RL can be used in optimization processes. For example, RL can assist in the material selection to find polymers that degrade more efficiently [122, 123]. Moreover, it can be used for the simulation of different synthesis conditions to obtain optimized materials [124, 125]. For further clarification, Figure 2.3 shows the example of how RL algorithms work, with a focus on their application in polymer science.

According to Figure 2.3, the RL algorithms are based on a cycle of actions done to get information about experimental observation. In the illustration, the agent (polymeric material used as a sample) suffers an action by the environment (mechanical resistance assay equipment) to provide an observation (response). Additionally, each action is associated with a reward (the investigation of the response of the polymeric material to the applied force) to classify whether this polymer can be either suitable or unsuitable for a specific application (e.g., in building, commercial materials, or as pieces of an automobile). Then, from repetition and sequential learning, the algorithm can make predictions of some polymeric properties and material classifications, that is, whether the polymer will be considered stable or recyclable. All these actions are performed by AI and operated by humans.

The use of RL in polymer discovery is supported by machine learning models that predict polymer properties, enabling the RL agents to make informed decisions based on predicted outcomes [126]. Thus, several studies have explored the application of RL in polymer degradation and recycling. To mention a few, two studies can be cited.

In the first study, the RL algorithm was used to synthesize polymers with enhanced thermal properties, such as thermal conductivity [127]. To carry out this type of study, dynamic simulations and different operational conditions, as well as high-quality and number of data, are required to get precise predictions. Additionally, in the second one, RL was used to perform cost analysis allied to polymer properties predictions [128]. Thus, with the aid of RL, it was possible to use agents capable of previewing scenarios (experimental conditions) that might result in undesirable outcomes for the polymers in industrial applications [129].

2.6 Conclusion

This chapter discussed the use of AI algorithms in polymer science over the years, bringing information on ML model categories and specific neural networks designed for time-series analysis. It was confirmed that the use of AI tools in polymer science is an emerging topic since it enables high applicability in real systems and in industrial-scale conditions. Thus, ML algorithms (e.g., clustering, RNN-LSTM, GRU, RF, XGB, DT, and SVM) have been continuously applied to predict polymer properties, as well as their degradation and recycling. Among these techniques, supervised AI algorithms have received particular attention in the field. Furthermore, characterization techniques (e.g., Raman spectroscopy, FTIR, dynamic light scattering, and computer vision) used to describe polymers can be valuable in constructing databases for AI algorithms applied to polymer science. The integration of AI with polymer science, along with the enhancement of key characterization techniques, can help reduce costs associated with the synthesis and commercialization of polymers, as well as decrease the time of bench-scale experiments, supporting optimization processes. As a perspective, the integration of AI with polymer science should be continuously encouraged, as it has the potential to enhance the efficiency of material design, accelerate the discovery of new polymers, and optimize experimental processes.

Chapter 3 Machine learning for material simulation: revolutionizing polymer science

Shikha Kumari
Pratima Parashar Pandey

Abstract

This chapter explains the role of machine learning in elevating polymer research, emphasizing on prediction of properties, material simulations, and the discovery of novel polymer configurations. Polymers pose unique challenges in simulations and experiments due to the complexity in their molecular structures and their varying properties. The traditional methods of polymer design rely greatly on experimental techniques that are based on large scale trial-and-error processes. These techniques are mostly costly and time-consuming. Machine learning offers a promising solution by providing powerful tools that can predict the properties of polymers before they are synthesized, which can drastically reduce the time and resource requirements. By utilizing vast datasets of experimental results and molecular descriptors, machine learning models can predict polymer properties such as mechanical strength, conductivity, thermal stability, and biodegradability with high accuracy. These predictive models can be used to quickly access all promising candidates of polymers and select the efficient one, thereby reducing the requirement of time-consuming and uneconomical experiments. Not only prediction, but machine learning can also support the design process for new polymer materials. Generative models such as variational autoencoders and generative adversarial networks are now being utilized to propose new polymer architectures with requisite properties. These models are capable of generating novel polymer structures that may not have been considered through traditional design methods. Additionally, reinforcement learning algorithms are being applied to optimize polymerization processes. By these algorithms, researchers can tweak parameters such as temperature, solvent, and pressure, which can further accelerate the design process by minimizing the number of experimental trials needed.

Keywords: Polymer science, machine learning, material simulation,

3.1 Introduction

Polymers are large molecules made by linking monomers together through covalent bonds. DNA and cellulose are naturally occurring polymers, while polyethylene and polystyrene are examples of manmade polymers. Polymer science is the study of polymers: that is, its synthesis, structure, properties, and applications [1, 2]. The unique characteristics of polymers such as flexibility, lightweight, strength and durability, and cost effectiveness have made them a vital component of modern technology and all fields of industries, including packaging [3], healthcare [4], electronics [5], automobile [6], and textile [7]. Despite numerous unique characteristics, the design and synthesis of polymers is very challenging that limits their performance. The prime limitations are in controlling the synthesis process, molecular structure, and properties of the polymer. Depending on the desired application of the polymer, its structure and properties like strength, flexibility, durability, etc. need to be tailored. Traditional practices require extensive trial and error until the desired polymer is synthesized, which can be time-consuming and costly [8]. Additionally, the polymerization process is also difficult to control; a small variation can cause significant change in the end product [9]. The stability and long-term performance of polymers requires prediction, which is also difficult to forecast using traditional methods. With increasing awareness toward environment and sustainability, the impact of certain synthetic polymers raises concern in relation to pollution [10, 11]. The traditional methods to recycle polymers degrade their characteristics, which limits their ability to be reused [12, 13, 14].

To address these challenges, technologies like machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are serving as essential tools. When applied to polymer science, they are enabling a fast and more accurate prediction of molecular structure, design, and synthesis of polymers. AI can process and analyze large databases and make predictions related to polymers more accurately, which can reduce time and cost considerably, in comparison to traditional trial-and-error-based methods [15, 16]. These technologies allow researchers to have more control over polymerization conditions like temperature, pressure, etc. Thus, researchers can predict right combinations to produce the desired polymers with the required properties. In addition, the technologies also optimize polymerization to improve the synthesis process. AI can also be useful in identifying recycling methods for polymer waste by examining the physical and chemical properties of the polymer [17]. To summarize, Al and ML are revolutionary tools to overcome the challenges of polymer science related to polymerization, synthesis, recycling, etc., making polymer science more efficient and sustainable. The rest of the chapter explains ML techniques and their applications to polymer science, and the challenges of AI and ML that limit their full utilization in the development of polymer technology. Lastly, how ML techniques can open new future directions in polymer science is discussed in detail.

3.2 Machine learning techniques in polymer science

AI is a field in computer science that is capable of performing tasks (e.g., reasoning, understanding, and problem solving) that require human intelligence. L is an interesting sub-branch of AI that analyzes and learns from available data and makes predictions and decisions, instead of following a strict set of instructions [18]. ML algorithms can learn using different approaches, which may include making decisions by directly studying the provided data or by analyzing hidden patterns within the data by taking feedback from the interacting environment [19] (see Figure 3.1 for better understanding of various ML algorithms).

Following are the key components of ML:

  1. Supervised learning – The model is prepared by using existing data, with known output known as labeled data.

  2. Unsupervised learning – The model is prepared using hidden patterns and structures within the data known as unlabeled data.

  3. Reinforcement learning (RL) – The model is prepared by receiving feedback from the interacting environment. The feedback can be in the form of benefits or punishments.

All these training methods can help build intelligent tools that can adapt and improve with time. AI and ML has become a vital component of our daily lives, with influence in transforming healthcare, customer experience, security enhancement, driving innovation, and facilitating research and technological development. The integration of ML with polymer science and engineering has accelerated the development of the branch, opening new research opportunities. ML has transformed this branch by making predictions, designing and optimizing new and more efficient polymers. The complete workflow of ML includes data processing, modeling, and validation (see Figure 3.2).

3.2.1 Supervised learning models

Supervised learning such as regression models, decision trees, and neural networks play a crucial role in predicting polymer properties. These models utilize the existing data on structure and properties of polymers to understand relationships and predicting new polymers with unknown properties. Regression techniques such as linear and polynomial regression models are also leveraged to predict the mechanical properties of polymers, such as tensile strength. Such models can relate chemical structures with macroscopic properties of the polymers. A recent study utilized a polynomial regression model to predict the mechanical properties of thermoplastic materials on the basis of their molecular structure [20]. Another supervised model used in polymer science is the decision tree. This algorithm breaks data into subsets, making them easier to understand and interpret. Numerous studies have employed decision trees to predict structural properties of polymers. One such study involves prediction of adhesive properties of polymer blends [21]. Artificial neural networks are another predictive model that is effective in determining biodegradability, thermal stability, and mechanical properties of polymers [22, 23]. The Polymer Genome is one such framework that offers effective tools that helps in this development [24]. The Polymer Genome is a computational tool that uses ML to analyze vast datasets of polymer molecular descriptors and experimental results to predict polymer properties such as mechanical strength, thermal stability, etc.

3.2.2 Deep learning models

Deep learning model is a powerful tool that can analyze complex data. It can understand complex nonlinear relationships in molecular structure and can handle high-dimensional molecular datasets. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are two such deep learning models that can identify complex molecular structure and predict behavior and properties of polymer for much more efficient material design. CNNs are efficient in processing grid-like data, making them suitable for understanding spatial hierarchies in molecular structures [25], while RNNs can analyze sequential data, making them suitable for understanding temporal dynamics in materials, making it suitable for understanding fracture propagation [26]. Thus, by using these two techniques, it is possible to predict potential energy surfaces and energy-conserving force fields, short-term local dynamics and long-term statistical properties of microstructures, and fracture prediction in brittle materials [27].

3.2.3 Generative models

Generative models are capable of generating novel polymer structures. These models can learn from existing data and discover new polymer structures with desired characteristics like conductivity, thermal stability, and biodegradability. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) and generative adversarial networks (GANs) are two such generative models that enable material designing with requisite properties, and have shown great advancements in computational material science. Both these models have several characteristics such as inverse design capabilities, where these models are capable of inverting the design process, which is practically impossible in traditional methods. These models can also enable exploration of the vast chemical spaces to uncover novel polymers that could not be identified using conventional approaches. These models can also learn from existing data to predict properties of novel polymers and provide efficient methods to speed up the discovery and optimization of materials.

VAEs can learn a low-dimensional latent space to replicate complex data distributions. These data distributions are then helpful in generating new data points. VAEs can analyze the existing polymer datasets and get trained by learning underlying patterns to generate novel polymer structures. VAEs, when combined with Gaussian process regression, can be used to design polymers with optimized properties for conditions like high temperatures and electric fields, which meet the required performance goals [28]. The GANs comprise two neural networks; a generator and a discriminator. Generator creates artificial data while discriminator distinguishes between authentic and artificial data. This adversarial process trains GANs to produce highly realistic data. GANs are also being used along with molecular dynamics simulations to create novel vitrimers. Vitrimers are a class of polymers that have dynamic bond exchange properties [29, 30]. In recent studies, GANs were combined with graph-based representations of polymers and this combination was capable of designing new polymer architectures that exhibit glass transition temperatures [29].

3.2.4 Reinforcement learning models

RL is a powerful tool that can optimize polymerization processes and speedup material design process by reducing the number of trials required in traditional experimental techniques. RL algorithms can be useful in adjusting variables such as temperature, pressure, and solvent characteristics to achieve requisite polymer properties. RL works on a feedback mechanism, where the algorithm interacts with the surrounding environment, adjusts the parameters, and receives feedback based on the outcomes [31]. This iterative loop continues till optimal polymerization conditions are achieved. Various studies where RL is trained to automate material synthesis and discovery are available in literature. Beeler et al. exploited a deep RL system to plan and execute chemical synthesis for creating novel materials [32]. There are studies where an RL-based approach is utilized for the solvent switch process in the pharmaceutical industry [33]. In this study, a digital twin is employed, which is a virtual representation of a physical process. This helps in fine-tuning the process parameters to achieve the desired results that enhance efficiency and reduce environmental impacts. All the different types of ML models that have been discussed above are summarized in Table 3.1.

3.3 Applications of machine learning in polymer research

In Section 3.2, the integration of ML and polymer research has been discussed in detail. By analyzing vast datasets available, the designing, synthesis, characterization, and optimization of polymers can be accelerated more efficiently. This section covers the applications of ML in polymer research:

  1. Design and property prediction: By analyzing existing datasets, ML can predict polymer properties like mechanical behavior, such as tensile strength, elasticity, and thermal and chemical properties. This information can help in designing new materials with the requisite properties that can considerably save time and efforts required in experimental trials [34]. This generally uses supervised learning and deep learning techniques.

  2. Optimization of synthesis: Polymer synthesis requires optimization of reaction conditions such as temperature, pressure, and catalysts, which is done by trial-and-error methods. These methods are time-consuming and costly. By analyzing experimental data, ML can identify optimal conditions for polymer synthesis [35]. This can significantly improve polymer quality and save lots of time and money.

  3. Characterization: The deep learning models in ML can be used to analyze spectroscopy data such as FTIR and NMR. By using these models, the morphology of the polymer like crystal structure, pore size distribution, and roughness can be assessed, and thus the characterization of the desired polymer can be improved [36].

  4. Lifetime prediction: ML models can analyze polymer degradation data to predict the lifetime of polymers. This information is important for polymers that have applications in automotive, aerospace, and packaging. These models predict the long-term behavior of polymers under various environmental conditions, which leads to more durable polymers [37, 38].

  5. Blends and composites: High-performance materials are usually created by combining multiple polymers together in a blend or composite. The combined properties of the polymers can create a highly efficient material with superior qualities, such as greater thermal resistance or high conductivity. High-performance plastics are examples of such a material. ML can be used here to predict the interactions among the various polymers and optimize the properties of polymer blend and composites [39].

  6. Polymer nanocomposites: Polymer nanocomposites are formed by the inclusion of nanoparticles on a polymer matrix. This is done to incorporate the characteristics of nanomaterials to enhance the properties of nanomaterials. ML can be used to predict the properties of these polymer nanocomposites and design enhanced nanocomposites [35, 40, 41].

  7. Environmental impact and recycling of polymers: To align with the global sustainability goals, it is necessary to shift toward sustainable polymers that are eco friendly [42, 43]. ML can help in this by predicting and classifying polymers based on their recyclability and optimizing the recycling process. The algorithm analyses the spectral data for this purpose.

3.4 Challenges and limitations

ML offers novel advancements in the development of polymer science, however there are several challenges that obstruct its full utilization. ML algorithms rely on high-quality and large datasets for better training and prediction. In polymer systems, due to the various molecular structures and properties, the datasets are complex and difficult to obtain. For example, new polymer families under development have limited data. Also, the sources of this data are diverse, including experimental data, data from research papers, etc. Such data lack proper format and uniformity required for ML models [44, 45]. Also, the model that is trained on a specific polymer dataset may not perform well when applied on another polymer dataset. Thus, the ability of the model to work on varied, new and unseen data remains a challenge.

Another major limitation of ML is that often tools like deep learning are visualized as black-box. The underlying mechanism that drives the material behavior is important in polymer science. However, the insights of how these models predict the polymer are not provided, making it difficult to verify the findings and thus, lacks trust [46, 47].

Applying ML to optimize the entire development process of polymer requires integration of models with the traditional experimental approaches [48]. This will ensure that the predictions are relevant and precise. Since experimental verification is based on trial and error, it is time-consuming and costly. Integrating it with ML for the training of the model, based on experimental feedback, can thus be a slow and iterative process. The hybrid models that combine ML and experimental data can be promising, but the success will depend on the quality of experimental data and the ability to integrate the data into ML models [49].

Combined efforts of computational researchers and experimentalists can help in overcoming these challenges in order to improve efficiency and drive innovation in polymer science.

3.5 Future directions and potential impact

In this section, we will discuss how the integration of ML in polymer science can impact its application in various industries and highlight key future directions in polymer science. ML techniques can open new opportunities in exploring material design and performance enhancement, promoting sustainability.

3.5.1 Advances in polymer design

ML models can be used to overcome challenges involved in polymer design. Hybrid model is a combination of deep learning, RL, genetic algorithm, and graph-based models. Deep Learning techniques are ideal in handling large unstructured datasets and predicting polymer properties [50], while RL can help in optimizing pathways to polymer synthesis. Graph-based methods can improve accuracy in both prediction and synthesis [51, 52]. The ability of hybrid models to combine multiple techniques together makes them more robust and versatile. Thus, they can handle the complexities and challenges involved in polymer design much better, providing more accurate and efficient design. Hybrid models can thus have a great potential in advancing polymer science, as they can help discover new materials with unknown properties and can also design polymers with requisite properties for specific applications.

3.5.2 Automated discovery of materials

AI has the potential of creating fully automated platforms that can predict, synthesize, and test polymers autonomously. AI-driven prediction models can be integrated with robotics or simulation systems to create such platforms that can do real-world testing. These systems will be capable of rapid assessment and prototyping of polymers that can accelerate the development of new polymers, which will be high performing, biocompatible, and sustainable. This can be beneficial for various industries, including medical science [53, 54].

3.5.3 Cross-disciplinary collaboration

AI can be fully utilized in polymer science when experts from various fields collaborate together to build an extensive far-reaching AI system that has deep scientific knowledge. Material scientists can contribute in understanding the output of the models, as they have expertise in polymer science. They can understand the structure, property, and behavior of polymers. Data scientists can focus on model selection, validity, and data processing, ensuring that the data is processed and analyzed appropriately, while chemists and engineers can provide insights of synthesis and polymerization processes for creating AI designs that mimic real-world labs. Thus, a strong collaboration between material scientists, data scientists, chemists, and engineers is required for the future of ML in the polymer industry [55].

3.5.4 Industrial implications

Integration of ML tools into polymer science can benefit multiple industries [56, 57]. The manufacturing industry can synthesize polymers at reduced cost that are more eco-friendly and sustainable, and produce less waste. The biomedicine industry can exploit AI tools to create polymers that are less toxic and biocompatible. These polymers can be used in tissue engineering, implants, and drug delivery. The electronics industry can leverage AI to design next-generation devices that are more flexible, with improved electrical, thermal, chemical and mechanical properties. All these technological advancements can break through existing bottlenecks and challenges in polymer science, revolutionizing manufacturing, biomedicine, electronics, packaging, aerospace, automobile, and many more industries.

3.6 Conclusion

ML plays a promising role in predicting the properties of polymers such as thermal stability, mechanical strength, conductivity, and biodegradability before their synthesis. Generative models such as VAEs and GANs are exploited to design specific polymer structures for particular application. This can save time, resources, and cost incurred during the experimental process. Also, these algorithms help in the optimization of the synthesized polymer by tweaking various parameters such as temperature, solvent, and pressure to help in making a tailored, desired polymer structure. Table 3.1 provides all the ML techniques used in polymer science. These different models are employed for various aspects of polymers. Regression techniques can relate chemical structures with macroscopic properties of the polymers. CNNs and RNNs are two deep learning models that can predict behavior and properties of polymers for much more efficient material design. Generative models can learn from existing data and invent new polymer structures with requisite characteristics like conductivity, thermal stability, and biodegradability desired for the particular application. RL is used in optimization of polymerization processes by reducing the time consumed in traditional experimental techniques. Further, it helps in characterization of polymer structure, durability of polymers under various environment conditions, and optimization of polymer nanocomposites properties. Using ML in polymer science achieves new heights despite many limitations in its implications due to unavailability of data in the proper format. Also, optimization needs to integrate various models into one, which is a slow and iterative process. But, the current scenario looks at AI for advancement in polymer design, collaboration in different disciplines, and industrial application along with an automated platform for new polymer structure in future.
