Chapter 8 AI-driven development: innovating biomedical polymer materials

Isha Kalbhor
Shantanu Chakote
Rushikesh Dabhade
Pranay Sharma
Sushant Gaikwad

ORCID:https://orcid.org/0000-0003-0284-8374

Raj Agarwal
Satish Polshettiwar

Conflict of interest: The authors do not have any conflict of interest.

Abstract

In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), polymeric biomaterials alter efficiency and precision in material design and properties. AI-driven models are leveraged for predicting, optimizing and developing novel biomaterials. A data-driven model for enhancing material properties may improve the development of polymeric biomaterials. This chapter depicts various AI-driven models, techniques, their advantages, and disadvantages for a robust and adequate AI model for innovating polymeric biomaterials. Advanced computational tools with AI-driven models for novel polymeric biomaterials may help researchers understand and redefine the landscape of biomedical polymers for innovating, patient-centric solutions in modern medicine.

Keywords: Biomaterials, artificial intelligence, deep learning, machine learning, polymers, reinforcement learning, predictive modeling,

8.1 Introduction

The current state of biomedical polymer research has been greatly influenced by the convergence of materials science and artificial intelligence (AI). The pharmaceutical industry is changing due to this intersection, particularly in drug systems for formulation, delivery, and discovery. Innovation in these key areas of the pharmaceutical industry is being driven using AI techniques in the design of biomedical polymers [1]. The rise of Industry 4.0, which is defined by the dominance of advanced digital technologies such as robots, big data analysis, and the Internet of Things (IoT), makes it easier to integrate AI-based design and production processes from start to finish. AI computer algorithms, for example, can optimize polymer formulas, and IoT sensors continuously monitor manufacturing to assure consistency and quality. Customized medication is made feasible by this partnership between AI and Industry 4.0, which enables a more effective, productive, and environmentally friendly approach for creating biomedical polymers and cutting-edge medical equipment [2, 3]. With the inclusion of AI in polymer designing, there is the potential to tap into vast design possibilities that are otherwise not achievable using traditional means [4]. ML algorithms can easily design novel polymer structures with special properties for targeted applications, for example, drug delivery devices to be implanted. This is of tremendous significance and plays an important role in addressing the growing need for specialized medical devices [5, 6]. Cooperation is an essential force to propel biomedical polymer innovation in solving new demands in the medical field [7, 8]. The continued emergence of such a technology is significant in its power to redefine pharmaceutical practice as well as alter the patient’s outcome with a more compounded medical landscape [9].

8.2 AI techniques in polymer discovery

The inclusion of AI in polymer discovery has changed the field of research, offering endless opportunities for innovation, optimization, and efficiency. Use of such techniques will enhance our ability to predict, optimize, and formulate within the field of polymer science.

  • Machine learning (ML) models have already shown a lot of potential in the field of research, as these algorithms act as the backbone of AI-driven advancements in polymer science. ML models can evaluate different sets of data, even those that may have complicated patterns, which can be applied in predictive modeling, high-throughput screening, and generative polymer design. It will drastically cut down on the time and expense involved in conventional experimentation [10]. The prediction of polymer properties and design optimization was achieved through the use of multiple ML models.

  • Supervised learning (SL) includes different types of training models based on labeled datasets, enabling it to learn known input–output relationships. Different types of algorithms, such as support vector machines (capture nonlinear relationships between molecular descriptors and polymer properties), random forests (uses a combination of decision trees, effectively handling the complex interactions between features), and gradient boosting (techniques such as XGBoost and LightGBM were used to enhance predictive accuracy), can be employed for property prediction and optimization. These techniques can be key to predicting properties like glass tensile strength and transition temperature [11]. For example, SVMs and RF can understand complex nonlinear relationships between polymer properties and molecular descriptors. Polymer property prediction, support vector machines achieved an R2 score of 0.85 for glass transition temperature, whereas it displayed a 0.80 R2 value for tensile strength. It elaborates about the capability of understanding molecular interactions responsible for thermal and mechanical properties, which makes it a valuable tool in polymer discovery [12].

  • Unsupervised learning (UL) includes principal component analysis (PCA) (aids in reducing the dimensionality of a large polymer dataset, which helps in feature selection and visualization), k-means clustering (groups polymers based on structural and physiochemical similarities, allowing for identification of novel polymer classes), and autoencoders (can be used for feature extraction and representation learning, enabling efficient classification). These algorithms deal with unlabeled data and play a crucial role in uncovering hidden structures or patterns without predefined outcomes, which allows researchers to explore unknown relationships [13].

  • Reinforcement learning (RL) includes generative adversarial networks (employed to generate new polymer structures with potentially useful properties), variational autoencoders (aids in exploring the latent space of polymer structure, leading to generation of innovative polymer candidates), and Bayesian optimization (optimizes polymer performance by effectively adjusting processing settings with minimal experimental work) [14]. RL incorporates decision-making into the learning process, allowing models to discover the best plan of action via trial and error. RL has demonstrated potential in optimizing polymer formulations and process conditions. For example, Reiser et al. [15] used active learning to design the polymer molecular weight distributions, gaining major improvements in computational efficiency and accuracy. Also, RL can be used to find the best polymer for specific use by continuously improving models based on feedback from previous results.

8.2.1 AI and ML for biomaterial applications

AI-driven advancements in polymer science are making their way in drastically with advanced techniques like computer simulations, high-throughput screening, and predictive models. There are a lot of techniques and algorithms that can be employed for biomaterial application figure 8.1, which were explained earlier. Table 8.1 summarizes different techniques that are used with respect to biomaterial applications.

Table 8.1:Different AI techniques with their biomaterial applications.

AI technique Application area in biomaterials
Supervised learning (RF and SVM) Property prediction, classification of materials by biocompatibility, and mechanical performance modeling
Unsupervised learning (PCA and k-means) Biomaterial clustering based on structural and functional properties, and feature extraction for predictive modeling
Deep learning (CNNs and RNNs) Microstructure analysis, predicting in vivo behavior, and processing condition optimization.
Reinforcement learning (RL) Optimizing synthesis processes and adaptive formulation tuning for smart biomaterials.
Generative models (GANs, VAEs) Designing novel polymers with tailored degradation rates, mechanical properties, and bioactivity

8.2.2 Computational techniques and high-throughput screening

Virtual testing and high-throughput screening: AI-powered virtual testing and high-throughput screening have also accelerated the search for novel polymers. These methods quickly assess and optimize candidate polymers using automated workflows and molecular dynamics simulations. They accomplish this by merging real-world experimental validations with insights from AI. According to Pyzer-Knapp et al. [13], integrating AI with HTS not only expedites the discovery process but also enhances the reliability of predictions by incorporating real-time data analysis and optimization.

8.2.3 Predictive modeling for polymer properties

Predictive modeling serves as the foundation for AI-mediated advancements in polymer science and provides remarkable capabilities for the prediction of material behavior and design optimization. CNNs are capable of analyzing microstructure images and abstracting hierarchical features for effective property predictions. GNNs describe molecular structure through graphs, exposing complex interactions in atoms and bonds to accurately predict polymer behavior [15]. Generative models operate in tandem with predictive modeling by generating new polymer structures with desired properties. GANs, as described by Goodfellow, engage in sequence minimax games to produce viable and diverse alternative designs. VAEs, while also generative models, differ from GANs in that they utilize a probabilistic method for navigating latent space, extend the possibilities for polymer design, and enable completely new material synthesis [16]. While progress has been made, there are still issues to overcome, particularly with data quality and algorithm designs. According to Himanen et al., “most datasets for polymers are either small, do not exhibit consistency, or do not have proper annotation”; these are all genuine issues for training good models. Future studies should aid in the cleaning and enriching of datasets, and most importantly, the collection of good experimental data, at appropriate resolutions for model training and validation. The refinement of methodologies and the development of hybrid models that leverage multiple ML techniques might also offer advantages in performance and help tackle long-standing issues related to overfitting and generalization [17]. The application of AI to polymer discovery represents a new frontier in material science that provides higher levels of predictive capability, faster innovations, and designs that are optimal. Through SL, UL, and RL algorithms, experienced practitioners can engage in partnerships with high-throughput screening for new polymers and utilize predictive models that will liberate the untapped promise of polymers for the benefit of scientists, and for use in initiatives across the sectors that utilize these materials and are so vital to all our endeavors. As we contend with a set of current and emerging issues, AI in polymers will change the landscape of our materials and their design and performance.

8.2.4 Data collection and preprocessing

To build robust ML models, multiple meaningful datasets are required. Figure 8.2 captures the overall polymer discovery process with further involvement of ML. The process of feature engineering was an integral step in converting raw data into descriptive variables that characterize the inherent chemical and structural properties of polymers [18]. Various molecular descriptors, including conventional topological indices and newer molecular fingerprints, were created using the RDK tools. In addition to the above, additional polymer-specific features, including chain length, branching topologies, and crosslinking density, were pulled from structure data to further enrich the feature set. In addressing the potential challenges stemming from working with a high-dimensional feature space and improving model interpretability, methods were used that preserved important information but reduced redundancy and noise in the data.

8.3 Applications for AI in biomedical polymers

8.3.1 Drug delivery system

The drug delivery system has experienced unprecedented developments over the years that have allowed it to deliver therapeutic agents in a targeted and effective way. One of the largest benefits of applying AI in healthcare delivery systems is its ability to handle and analyze huge amounts of data. This kind of analysis enables researchers to know how different components of a formulation interact, their concentrations separately, and how they are all responsible for drug delivery efficacy [19].

AI can analyze many sources of data, including chemical structures, physicochemical descriptors, and bioactivity data, to find key associations. With trend identification and pattern discovery, AI could play a vital role in making efficient drug delivery systems and thus making them more safe and stable [20]. Utilizing the strength of AI along with large sets of data, scientists can hasten the development of safe and effective drug delivery systems, improving patient outcomes and advancing the field of pharmaceutical sciences [21].

8.3.2 Intelligent nanocarriers

Colloidal drug carrier systems with particle sizes less than a micrometer are referred to as nanocarriers. AI methods are often suggested as solutions to a range of nanotechnology issues. These are the development of nanosystems, nanocomputing, and the use of AI approaches to the development of simulation methods at the nanoscale. Several AI-based methods are being suggested to predict the effectiveness of drug combinations using pharmacological synergies. Employing various types of nanoparticles to enhance drug localization at tumor sites, potential avenues for AI optimized optimization in combination drug delivery are being explored in this field [22]. One of the potential areas of drug delivery research is nanocarrier design and optimization for targeted drug delivery, and AI algorithms can greatly enhance their performance. Scientists can develop predictive models that consider a variety of variables like the physicochemical properties of nanocarriers, pharmacological characteristics, and biological parameters using AI algorithms [23]. For optimal drug delivery, these models can be used to select the appropriate nanocarrier composition, size, surface modification, and other formulation characteristics. Combinatorial drug design is maximized through an AI-driven feedback system control (FSC) platform, specifically in treating cancer with nanocarriers. Surface properties of nanocarriers play a very vital role in determining their stability, bioavailability, and cellular dispersion and absorption within the body. AI supports the analysis and prediction of the effects of surface alterations, for example, ligand conjugation or the deposition of targeting molecules, on cell–nanocarrier interaction. It decides the best ligands or method using molecular and cellular data. The aim in combining automation and AI is to increase the tailoring of targeted therapeutic nanocarriers for cell types and individual patients [24].

8.3.3 Smart drug delivery

AI has an important function in the design of sophisticated drug delivery systems that respond to physiological cues or health conditions [25]. AI programs facilitate continuous monitoring and control of drug release from these delivery systems. Through the evaluation of tailored patient data, for example, blood drug concentration, physiological metrics, or biomarkers, AI programs can provide expert advice regarding drug dosage, scheduling, and release rates. They can constantly analyze the collected data and adjust the drug release profile accordingly. Additionally, AI assists in the formulation of injectable drug delivery systems using thermosensitive hydrogels, which are sensitive to temperature changes. With ML algorithms, researchers can forecast the behavior of intricate polymer compositions under various conditions of the surrounding environment. With this capability, controlled drug delivery is formulated for prolonged periods. Furthermore, the combination of AI and wearable technology, biosensors, or sensors make it possible to deliver drugs for the purpose of delivering customized and dynamic therapies, resulting in enhanced therapeutic responses [26].

8.3.4 Tissue engineering scaffolds

Tissue engineering scaffolds play a critical role in the practice of regenerative medicine, as they provide the structural support required for cell attachment, proliferation, and differentiation [27]. The incorporation of AI into scaffold design, biomaterial optimization, and predictive modeling has greatly enhanced the efficiency and clinical translation of tissue-engineered constructs. In various applications AI can be leveraged for tissue engineering applications.

8.3.4.1 AI-based material selection and design

AI employs ML algorithms to forecast the mechanical and biological characteristics of polymers in terms of variables such as molecular structure, cross-linking density, and degradation rates. AI models determine the interaction between biomaterials and cells, forecasting biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and degradation patterns. AI platforms like ChemSpider interpret chemical compositions to screen the best candidate for scaffold production.

8.3.4.2 Prediction of scaffold mechanical properties

AI greatly promotes the molecular and chemical optimization of tissue engineering scaffolds by predicting material properties, directing scaffold design, and optimizing chemical functionalization. ML models evaluate large datasets to estimate elasticity, porosity, and load-bearing capacities, while AI algorithms assess the effect of motifs and functional groups on cell adhesion, protein adsorption, and overall scaffold performance [28].

8.3.4.3 In silico prediction

Finite element modeling (FEM), in association with design strategies such as triply periodic minimal surfaces and signed distance field (SDF), enables in silico prediction of mechanical response. FEM simulations help fine-tune the pore and structure dimensions to achieve the required scaffold architecture, thus improving both mechanical and degradation properties [28].

8.3.4.4 Hydrogel and composite scaffold design

AI forecasts the self-assembly of peptide hydrogels, which are popular in tissue engineering for their biocompatibility and biodegradability. AI assists in comprehending and tuning the nontrivial interaction between peptide sequence and hydrogel properties.

8.3.4.5 Optimization of 3D printing parameters

AI could optimize 3D printing parameters for tissue engineering scaffolds, resolving issues involving material selection, process control, and minimizing defects. AI methods can improve the accuracy, efficiency, and reliability of 3D-printed scaffolds, in turn resulting in enhanced tissue regeneration and clinical performance [29].

8.3.4.6 Polymeric bioinks

AI models evaluate the printability of different polymeric bioinks based on critical parameters, such as viscosity, curing behavior, and mechanical stability. Identification of suitable printing conditions for new materials is usually a time-consuming and resource-scarce endeavor, requiring copious experimentation. AI can help mitigate this challenge by analyzing the underlying behaviors existing within a given dataset [30].

8.3.4.7 Process parameter optimization

AI algorithms adjust numerous process parameters such as nozzle diameter, extrusion rate, temperature, and pressure to produce scaffolds with exact dimensions [31]. The potential of AI to process large amounts of complex data, perform complex calculations, automate processes, learn from history, and optimize operations on an ongoing basis makes it a crucial resource [32].

8.3.4.8 Patient-specific scaffolds

AI promotes the creation of patient-specific scaffolds through controlling and adjusting printing parameters, offering feedback, and having sufficient data for reproducibility. Incorporating AI helps predict, adjust, and manage parameters, which reduces the scope for errors and improves customization of scaffolds [31].

8.4 Medical diagnostics and biosensors

Medical diagnostics are not only crucial for the care of individual patients but also for the prevention, screening, and monitoring of many diseases and conditions [33]. They cover a broad range of tools and methods, ranging from laboratory tests (in vitro diagnostics) to imaging tests [34]. AI systems utilize ML algorithms to efficiently and accurately evaluate medical images. This essential feature helps with the early diagnosis of hard-to-diagnose diseases. Early detection of such conditions is important, as it can lead to instant interventions, thus having the potential to save lives and enhance treatment outcomes. Furthermore, AI has opened new avenues in the areas of quantification and image segmentation. Using sophisticated algorithms, AI can identify regions of interest in medical images, such as tumors, vessels, and cells, with remarkable accuracy. Such image segmentation plays a pivotal role in treatment planning since it enables medical professionals to precisely define intervention areas, optimize surgical procedures, and deliver therapies that are directed to specific regions [35].

AI system helps radiologists identify breast cancer more precisely, rapidly, and uniformly. Such AI systems learn thousands of de-identified mammograms and hence recognize the subtle signs that represent indications of cancer, perhaps detecting warning signs that may not be recognized by experts. It is used to examine CT scans to detect lung nodules, which can signal lung cancer. This technology has been promising in enhancing rates of detection and helping radiologists detect both benign and malignant nodules [36].

Previously, applications of AI in nodule detection utilized conventional computer-aided design (CAD) strategies, but subsequent developments have utilized advanced DL methodologies such as CNNs [37]. Earlier research on CAD for pulmonary nodule diagnosis with chest X-ray has reported high false-positive rates and sensitivity as low as 52%. But the use of AI in combination with contemporary methods for detecting pulmonary nodules in radiographs has improved sensitivity to a level of 70–90%, comparable to that of radiologists, while reducing false-positive rates to 0.3–2.0 per radiograph [38].

AI shows substantial promise in improving the performance and efficiency of radiologists in detecting and analyzing lung nodules. Improvements in AI algorithms and a rise in imaging volumes will propel the creation and use of AI in clinical environments. Depending on its implementation, AI can benefit patients by mitigating uncertainty from indeterminate lung nodules but also potentially risk harm by introducing unnecessary diagnostic work. In addition, AI creates new challenges for radiologists, including higher IT demands and potential liability concerns. Developing strong technological and regulatory infrastructures will enable the incorporation of AI algorithms into clinical practice, ultimately resulting in beneficial impacts on patient health [39].

The incorporation of AI into medical imaging has significantly improved the field of personalized medicine. Through the analysis of medical images along with patient information, AI algorithms can produce insights specific to each patient. This ability allows for the creation of customized treatment protocols that consider individual differences in anatomy, physiology, and disease profiles [40].

A personalized model of healthcare not only optimizes the efficacy of therapies but also minimizes the likelihood of undesirable side effects, leading to improved patient outcomes and an improved quality of life [41]. AI-based algorithms significantly increase the function of biosensors through enhanced interpretation of information [42].

Polymers used in biosensors are bound to specific biomarkers, while AI algorithms treat the sensor data to recognize patterns and predict biological changes, making the sensors more sensitive and accurate. ML techniques and DL, cleanse sensor data from noise and enhance the quality of signals, thus setting the trustworthiness of biosensors. Computer simulations accelerated by AI accelerate research and development of new biomedical polymers by offering quicker prototyping and testing. Researchers employ computer software to simulate the interaction between different polymer materials and cells, tissues, and body fluids with diseases and other health conditions, minimizing big animal tests and accelerating the design of new diagnostic devices based on polymers [41]. For example, nanocomposites that combine polymers with materials like graphene and carbon nanotubes have AI-assisted analysis to maximize their electrical conductivity and surface area for the enhancement of the sensitivity of biosensors.

The ability of AI to forecast and optimize the properties of nanocomposites is realized as enhanced biosensor performance in terms of sensitivity, selectivity, repeatability, and stability. AI is necessary for the development of smart biosensors with the capability of adapting to changing biological environments. Glucose sensors based on polymers for diabetic patients can be improved using AI algorithms that measure glucose levels and predict future variations to allow active condition management. This adaptability encompasses wearable sensors that measure health parameters such as heart rate and oxygen saturation continuously, giving immediate feedback to clinicians and patients. These smart biosensors also comprise operational polymers that respond to physiological parameters, such as pH or glucose concentration, to deliver medication or provide feedback. AI improves these systems by predicting optimal rates of drug release and monitoring the effectiveness of the treatment in real time. AI assists in the design of long-term stable implantable sensors with high mechanical and biological compatibility. The sensors employ flexible polymers to obtain a tissue mimetic structure, which allows real-time monitoring of physiological data from within the body. Short-term implantable devices have been developed to allow high throughput drug sensitivity testing in solid tumors. The implantable microsystems for personalized anticancer therapy project aims to create implantable wireless sensors to track tumor oxygen levels in real time. Table 8.2 provides the advantages of the application of AI and ML in biomaterials.

Table 8.2:AI and ML applications in biomaterials.

Application Description Benefits
Material design AI algorithms forecast material characteristics, thereby refining designs for uses Accelerated development and enhanced material efficacy
Biosensor development AI improves sensitivity and
specificity of biosensors by evaluating sensor data and anticipating biological variations		 Enhanced diagnostic precision and continuous monitoring
Tissue engineering AI refines the design and production of scaffolds, promoting tissue regeneration Tailored scaffolds and better tissue integration
Drug delivery systems AI fine-tunes drug release profiles and bioavailability, thereby increasing treatment effectiveness Enhanced drug targeting and reduced side effects

8.5 Advantages of AI-driven development in biomaterials and manufacturing

There are various advantages of AI in polymer manufacturing and development, which speed up the process and become an integral part of the industries [43, 44]. Certain advantages of the AI in polymer manufacturing and the ML are given below.

8.5.1 Advantages in biomaterial research

  1. Process optimization for manufacturing

    AI proved as an efficient and cost-effective tool in manufacturing biomaterials using optimization parameters such as shaping, molding, 3D printing, and heat treatment.

  2. Improved materials design and their synthesis

    AI analyzes large material properties databases and their correlation to generate new materials designs of specific characteristics. This helps in innovating materials having good performance and biocompatibility. In fields like tissue engineering and drug delivery this advantage is valuable.

  3. Better interpretation and image analysis

    AI can analyze medical images, biomaterial images, help in diagnosis, monitor, and treat the disease while evaluating material performance and integrity. This is especially used for analyzing complex data.

  4. Quicker material finding and predictive modeling

    Traditional trial and error in the experiment is considerably reduced by this predictive capability [43]. AI can utilize large datasets of material properties and accelerated material discovery by predicting biocompatibility, degradation rates, and characteristics of biomaterials.

  5. Overcoming obstacles in the study of biomaterials

    AI is beneficial in various aspects of biomedical polymer manufacturing, but there are challenges such as quality and limited data availability [44]. However, improvement in model interpretation and the development and standardization of datasets are gradually solving these issues.

8.5.2 Advantages in polymer manufacturing

  1. Enhanced manufacturing processes

    Application of AI in polymer production process includes various stages, which are maintenance, production scheduling, monitoring, and production manufacturing. Hence AI is useful in improving overall efficiency and optimization.

  2. Improved structural design and their properties

    AI can discover novel materials and enhance accessibility of existing ones. AI improves structural design and polymeric characteristics.

  3. High optimization capacity and 24/7 availability

    AI algorithms provide high optimization and are available whenever required, which helps in maximum production and reducing downtime

  4. Advanced analytical features and fast decision-making

    AI provides advanced analytical capabilities and facilities faster decision-making in polymer manufacturing, in the end increasing productivity and efficiency in polymer manufacturing.

  5. Application across diverse industries

    AI greatly impacts polymer manufacturing in industries such as food, cosmetics, healthcare, dentistry and agriculture. For example, AI helps in managing quality control, supply chain, and cleaning process in food industry. In dentistry AI supports bio implants planning and the development of new dental materials.

  6. Addressing challenges in polymer manufacturing

    There are various advantages of AI in polymer manufacturing. Despite the advantages polymer production processes face AI- related challenges, which include high initial costs, potential job displacement, and the need for clear production strategies. But the efficient production quality and the long-term benefits overcome these obstacles.

8.5.3 Advantages in custom manufacturing

  1. Flexible production methods

    Without human involvement, AI itself is flexible in optimizing manufacturing processes and maintains optimal performance instantly responding to changes in production and material properties. It is an essential advantage for low volume and customized manufacturing.

  2. Improved machining precision

    AI-enhanced precision helps in decreasing errors in computer numerical control (CNC) machining by optimizing tool paths, resulting in higher-quality products and reduced material waste.

  3. Real-time quality control

    AI-driven vision system conducts real time quality control, identifying manufacturing defects early and reducing waste and rework.

  4. Predictive analysis

    To predict customer demand AI uses real-time data and history trends to minimize waste and optimize inventory levels. It is beneficial in the rapidly evolving automotive industry.

  5. Predictive maintenance

    AI algorithm predicts equipment failures, enabling planned maintenance during off peak hours, reducing downtime, lowering maintenance cost, and extending equipment life span.

  6. Addressing challenges in custom manufacturing

    Adding AI into custom manufacturing presents challenges such as system compatibility, data security, and workforce adaptation. However, phase integration, employee training, and cloud-based solutions help mitigate these issues.

8.6 Generative AI for novel polymer structure

The models use machines to design new polymer forms and predict the results they will have [45]. This type of model is data-powered, and it learns from the data, not just theory. It can induce novel types of molecular structures optimized for high strength and toughness, with progress sustained only through circulation within a supportive ecosystem, or through biologically degradable intelligence committed to maintaining engagement with emerging possibilities. And it makes good paraphernalia for many different activities in industry as well – healthcare systems overview of generative models: Machine knowledge of polymer structures has been applied to predicting outcomes for medical applications such as drug delivery, tissue engineering, and self-healing materials, thereby enhancing the efficacy of new materials research and design. The “new beast” of machine knowledge models called generative AI can produce innovative, synthetic data which is very similar to realistic data. Many fields, like chemistry and knowledge of polymers have been transformed by these models.

8.6.1 Generative adversarial network (GAN)

GANs are also being increasingly utilized in designing biomedical polymers wherein two neural networks (the generator and discriminator) are used for data generation and classification, respectively. This approach is convenient for designing new biomedical polymer architectures. While doing these tasks, the discriminator analyzes the candidate polymers that the generator suggests for possible biomedical uses. The development cycle of new medical devices can be accelerated by using GANs to refine polymer characteristics by verifying that the produced polymers are biocompatible and functional.

GANs are a type of deep generative model first proposed by Goodfellow et al., designed to generate high-quality synthetic data by capturing essential structural features from input data and associating them with desired properties. The foundation of GANs stems from the two main building blocks, the generator and the discriminator, which are fixed at opposition with each other. The generator has to extract locally meaningful features to output realistic data unlike the discriminator that tries to identify if the sample has been taken from the real dataset or generated by a model. GANs are trained such that their generated samples are indistinguishable from true data by the discriminator. The goal of GANs is to generate data that is indistinguishable from real samples to the discriminator. In the field of biomedical polymers, GANs have been used to generate molecular structures, and their adversarial training mechanism can be used to solve complex nonlinear formulation problems in various fields and can also be applied to UL tasks. These capabilities enable GANs to contribute to data generation and material design processes within polymer science.

8.6.2 Common models of GANs

Many improved GAN models were proposed to achieve more stable and better performance. As an example, deep convolutional GANs (DCGANs) use convolutional layers in place of fully connected layers, leading to a near-symmetrical structure of the generator and the discriminator. What this design accomplishes is substantially more stable training and higher quality samples. The Kullback-Leibler divergence is often used to ensure the generated distribution becomes close to the true distribution, thus preventing the mode collapse problem, which is common in standard GANs, leading to more diverse and realistic output.

8.6.3 Graph neural network (GNN)

GNNs have found extensive applications in biomedical polymer research since they can model complex molecular structures and capture the relationships between atoms and bonds [46]. GNNs rely on passing messages back and forth between nodes and edges before updating a node; all information from neighboring nodes and edges is aggregated before it is used to update the node representation, where the nodes represent atoms and edges represent bonds in a molecular graph, GNNs are a strong way to represent the structure of molecules. Although SMILES strings offer compact representations of polymer monomers, critical information like hybridization states, stereochemistry, and 3D connectivity is largely lost. Molecular graphs, on the other hand, capture these structural relationships directly, and thus are better fit for machine learning.

As GNN research progresses, various GNN variants, including graph convolutional networks (GCNs), gated graph neural networks (GGNNs), and message passing neural networks (MPNNs), have been used for molecular representation. These models have traditional molecular feature extraction methods, such as Morgan fingerprints, by providing richer molecular representations. When combined with techniques like extreme gradient boosting (XGB), GNNs further improve predictive performance. Deep learning models typically require large datasets, but in polymer research, particularly for newly discovered polymers, available datasets are often sparse. This data scarcity hinders the model’s ability to fully capture the latent structural features of polymers, making accurate property prediction difficult. To overcome this limitation, Guo et al. proposed the Meta-MGNN model, which applies few-shot learning techniques to enhance GNN performance in low-data scenarios.

8.6.4 Deep neural network (DNN)

Basic ML models are increasingly inadequate for analyzing the vast and complex data associated with biomedical polymers, especially given the expanding range of applications and data types. Advanced machine learning techniques are becoming insufficient for analyzing data related to biomedical polymers due to their increasing complexity and volume. In biomedicine polymers, input molecular structural descriptors are fed into the model, while output target features are biocompatibility or mechanical strength. Metaheuristic optimization strategies such as genetic algorithms (GA) and Bayesian optimization (BO) are often applied to adjust the rest of the hyperparameters such as the number of hidden layers, neurons per hidden layer, and learning rates, to enhance model accuracy and stability. The model is continuously retrained with updated hyperparameters, leading to higher stability and improved accuracy of the model.

8.6.5 Recurrent neural networks (RNNs)

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) stand out for their ability to integrate various types of sequential data, such as polymer breakdown, drug release activity, and chemical sequence analysis for neural network applications in polymers. RNNs can model the interdependence of the structure of a polymer monomer and its properties effectively. The sequence of atomic bonding within a polymer has an important impact on its structure-property relationships [47]. Molecular structures can be represented using sequences that treat each chemical fragment as a character within a sequence. Given their capability to capture long-term dependencies within sequences, RNNs can explore the intrinsic influence of atomic arrangements on the properties of polymers. This enables the construction of highly accurate predictive models for polymer properties by feeding SMILES strings as input and predicting specific polymer features as outputs.

8.6.7 Variational autoencoders (VAEs)

VAEs are a class of deep latent space-generative models that have shown considerable success across numerous biomedical informatics applications, including polymer structure prediction, medical image classification and segmentation, protein design, molecular design, and multi-omics data analysis. Polymers, critical across numerous sectors, including in pharmaceuticals and biomedical devices, face significant limitations in terms of the diversity of commercially available materials. Considerable time and financial investment have been directed toward developing novel biomedical polymers to address the shortcomings of existing medical-grade materials. ML, particularly VAEs, offers an unprecedented opportunity to accelerate the discovery process by reducing the reliance on traditional trial-and-error synthesis approaches.

VAEs can facilitate the rapid design and optimization of polymer properties using minimal experimental data, significantly shortening development timelines. High-throughput screening techniques can be employed for directly assessable properties, such as water uptake or cytotoxicity, enabling rapid dataset generation for model training. These high-throughput approaches, when combined with data-efficient techniques such as Bayesian optimization or active learning, can further accelerate polymer discovery processes. High-throughput methods have already demonstrated promise in polymer excipient design and antibacterial polymer discovery within regenerative medicine. Applying machine learning to biomedical polymer development can benefit from datasets generated through such methods, particularly when properties like mechanical strength or processing characteristics require larger sample sizes. However, high-throughput polymerization techniques have primarily focused on chain-growth polymerizations (including ring-opening polymerization and reversible addition-fragmentation chain transfer polymerization), which are widely used in medical polymers. There remains a notable lack of high-throughput techniques for step-growth polymerizations, which are critical for producing polymers such as poly (lactic acid) (PLA), polyurethanes, and nylons used in sutures, medical tubing, and short-term implants. Developing scalable high-throughput techniques for these processes would significantly enhance the available data for ML-driven biomedical polymer development [48, 49].

8.7 Other approaches for polymer development

AI-driven molecular modelling techniques, such as density functional theory and Monte Carlo simulations, play a crucial role in simulating the behavior of polymer molecules at the atomic scale. These simulations help researchers understand how different monomers and polymerization techniques influence key material properties such as tensile strength, thermal stability, and biodegradability.

8.7.1 Data-driven approaches

An increasing number of correlations between molecular features and characteristic material characteristics have been observed via machine learning models, generated from very large datasets of the structure and properties of polymers. These approaches may be used for predicting and developing properties of polymeric biomaterials.

8.7.2 AI-driven molecular modelling in polymer design

Based on the literature survey, the AI-driven molecular modelling for polymer design can be used for the following purposes:

  1. Polymer property prediction: Applied researchers may develop predictive models for a variety of polymer properties (tensile strength, melting point, and glass transition temperature) using machine learning approaches. Computational simulations or experimental data may be employed to train these models.

  2. Monomer screening and design: AI algorithms can screen many potential monomers and decide whether they can be used to produce sustainable polymers. The AI system can also tailor monomer combinations for improving properties of interest, such as biodegradability or recyclability, to achieve the desired characteristics.

  3. Structure–property relationships: ML models might derive structure-property relations, which otherwise remain unbreakable. Downloaded data about models, predictions, and materials approach can also provide insight into how polymer-specific structures impact the performance of these materials in the end-use applications [49].

  4. Innovative polymer structure: Self-healing polymers are polymers that can repair themselves when they are damaged. They depend on natural mechanisms that are similar to human skin, and have an innate capacity to repair themselves. Reversible polymer chemistry of polymers in the past has emerged as a promising route, with many examples of self-healing polymer systems being reported. Called “mendomers” or “dynamers,” these special polymers are composed of reversible bonds, formatted to respond to environmental conditions, including heat, light, and acidic conditions. This unique behavior has demonstrated effective self-healing polymeric action. Therefore, the potential for a mendomer to continuously heal itself resembles the restoration of the original material. The reversible bonds in mendomers can be engineered to act as weak links that break under stress, thereby preserving the stability of permanent bonds – a crucial aspect for self-healing processes [50]. The market trend in self-healing materials, particularly in the USA, is driven by the presence of multinational companies investing in ongoing research and development to discover cutting-edge technologies. The application of advanced expertise to expand product portfolios assists in capturing untapped markets by increasing the customer base [51]. These materials reduce the frequency and maintenance required for damage repair, which is expected to be a key driver of market growth [52].

8.8 Ethical considerations and regulatory challenges for AI in polymer science

Integrating AI and ML in polymer science provides new horizons of opportunities and innovations [53, 54]. But this convergence also poses some regulatory challenges that need to be prudently addressed. This discussion will emphasize data privacy and security, the ethical implications of AI in developing materials, and building regulatory frameworks.

8.8.1 Data privacy and security

AI for polymer science depends highly on large datasets for properties, synthesis, and applications of the materials. Sensitive data may be contained within these data that may pose a threat to data security and privacy. So, any data to do with how you formulate a chemical, how it’s manufactured, and what you use it for, especially in sensitive areas like health care or national security, could be targeted for unauthorized access or misuse.

Data breaches can be so harmful; therefore, they require tight security and regular security audits. Beyond that, anonymization or pseudonymization methods need to be used to safeguard individuals’ or organizations’ privacy while inserting their data into AI models. It is crucial to be transparent regarding the usage of data and how to deal with the data [57]. Using only relevant data protection rules, such as the General Data Protection Regulation or the California Consumer Privacy Act and complying to them is critical.

8.8.2 Ethical implications of AI in material developmen

There are various ethical challenges in the deployment of AI for material design and development. The possibility of bias in AI algorithms is one of the biggest problems. It is important to point out that these recommendations and predictions can reinforce and even exaggerate the existing biases in case the training data reflects existing biases [55]. The creation of information that is harmful to certain societal groups or the environment can have unforeseen adverse impacts. For example, instead of promoting sustainable production, a biased algorithm may optimize for cost-effectiveness, producing products with adverse environmental impacts [57]. The potential for AI to speed up the development of multiple uses of materials raises another ethical concern. But compounds that are attractive to law enforcement will also have possible uses that should raise concerns, such as their potential to be turned into weapons or used wrongfully. Risks associated with dual-use materials need to be carefully considered to prevent unwanted effects.

8.8.3 Establishing regulatory frameworks

Considering the rapid progress of AI in polymer science, a proper regulatory framework to deal with potential hazards and ethical issues must be built. So, this framework should be adaptable enough to handle the changing nature of AI technology, while providing sufficient security for individuals, society, and the environment [54]. There are several vital decisions that must be made when developing these frameworks:

  • Algorithmic account and transparency: Here, to enable examination and accountability, laws must require the transparency of algorithms used in AI systems. This could help in locating and reducing any possible errors or mistakes in the models [55].

  • Data management and safety guidelines: For the protection of sensitive data used in AI models, specific data management and security guidelines are needed. So basically, these guidelines must be followed for data collection, processing, storage, and exchange [56].

  • Risk assessment and reduction: Thorough risk assessment procedures that identify possible risks and suggest ways for reducing them should be part of regulatory frameworks for AI-driven material development. This would prevent unintended consequences and ensure responsible innovation [56].

  • Ethical review boards: It is necessary to develop ethical review boards, especially for the production of AI-driven products that can make sure that moral issues are taken into account during the stages of research and development while ensuring fair monitoring [55].

Policies concerning AI in polymer science require changes to meet new challenges. Effective policymaking, ethical consideration, and industrial engagement need collaboration to ensure that potential harms are mitigated, ethical standards are met, and the benefits of AI are maximized. A more developed response to the challenges and risks of a swiftly evolving environment is supplied by more proactive and flexible planning and policy making [55].

8.9 Future directions

With a variety of possible developments in the works, the future of AI-driven polymer design is bright:

8.9.1 Integration of AI with high-throughput experimentation

Finding new sustainable polymers will be accelerated by combining AI with high-throughput screening methods, which will allow for the efficient testing of several polymer candidates in a short time [58].

8.9.2 Multiscale modeling

Future AI models could use information from several scales, such as macroscopic material properties or molecular dynamics simulations, to provide a more thorough knowledge of polymer behavior.

8.9.2 Quantum computing

The development of quantum computing can transform molecular simulations, making it feasible to model even more complicated polymer systems and speeding the creation of sustainable polymers.

8.9.3 Enhanced machine learning models

The accuracy and reliability of ML models will continue to improve as more extensive and standardized datasets become available. Advances in processing power and algorithms will enable the development of increasingly sophisticated models, facilitating the exploration of complex material behaviors and interactions. For example, combining ML with high-throughput screening techniques can significantly accelerate the discovery of novel materials with desired properties [59].

8.9.4 Lipid–polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPHNPs)

LPHNPs represent a transformative class of nanodrugs with substantial therapeutic potential in translational biomedical research. These hybrid systems offer distinct advantages over conventional delivery approaches, including enhanced selectivity for targeted delivery, improved biological responses, and better safety profiles. Most LPHNPs exhibit prolonged circulation times, allowing for effective accumulation at the desired target site. The increasing focus on combinatorial cancer therapies further highlights the significance of LPHNPs, which act as multifunctional platforms capable of both simultaneous imaging and drug delivery (theranostics). Additionally, with the rise of gene therapy, LPHNPs are being actively explored as nonviral gene delivery vectors, demonstrating versatility across a wide range of therapeutic applications.

Given the rapid advancements over the past decade, LPHNPs are expected to gradually replace conventional liposomes and polymeric nanoparticles in therapeutic delivery systems. The exponential growth of research focused on hybrid systems, especially studies investigating diverse surface modifications and tunable cargo loading techniques, further underscores their potential. Ongoing research is expected to lead to even more innovative applications, solidifying the versatility of LPHNPs for safe and targeted drug delivery [59, 60].

8.9.5 Polymer science and nanotechnology integration

Although polymer science has a rich history spanning several decades, it continues to captivate scientists worldwide. The integration of nanotechnology with polymer science holds the potential to revolutionize numerous fields by harnessing the unique benefits of both disciplines. Through nanotechnology, polymers can be engineered at the nanoscale, introducing fascinating optical, electrical, and magnetic properties, thereby enhancing their versatility for a wide range of applications.

Polymer science offers extensive research opportunities in diverse areas, including polymer electronics, biopolymers, mechanophores (molecular units that alter polymer properties in response to mechanical forces), smart and reactive polymers, self-cleaning polymers, and self-healing polymers. Polymer nanoparticles hold considerable promise as future building materials, raw materials for 3D printing, packaging materials, polymer electrolytes, polymer lasers, flame-retardant materials, advanced catalysts, and components for next-generation electrochemical devices. The future of polymer science is bright, with transformative innovations anticipated at the interface of nanotechnology and polymer science.

8.10 Conclusion

The integration of AI into biomedical polymer materials has revolutionized the field, offering innovative solutions for the development of advanced materials with enhanced biocompatibility, mechanical properties, and targeted functionalities. AI-driven methodologies have demonstrated their ability to optimize material design, streamline synthesis processes, and accelerate the discovery of novel biomaterials tailored for medical applications. This chapter may be helpful for researchers, biomedical engineers, and regulatory authorities. AI-driven methodologies may further be used for predictive analysis of mechanical and biological properties, targeted drug delivery, screening purposes, personalized medicine, and novel biomaterials design.
