Chapter 10 Artificial intelligence in polymer molding and extrusion

Jatinder Singh Dhaliwal
Pravesh Kumar
Rajesh M. Badhe
Alex C. Pulikottil
Alok Sharma

Abstract

Polymer injection molding and extrusion are critical production techniques for manufacturing plastic parts, which play a vital role in industries like industrial goods, automotive, electronics, healthcare, sports, construction, and consumer products. Producing high-quality molded products requires precise control over factors such as injection pressure, speed, and mold design. Traditionally, defect detection in molding depends on operator’s experience, making quality control less efficient. Likewise, polymer extrusion is a vital technique for manufacturing plastic products like pipes, films, fibers, and profiles, involving stages such as plasticization and shaping. However, maintaining high-quality standards in both molding and extrusion presents a challenge, as accurate and automated defect detection remains difficult. Conventional methods are labor-intensive and heavily reliant on human judgment.

Research has demonstrated that intelligent manufacturing can address these challenges by optimizing process parameters for consistent and efficient molding and extrusion. Hybrid approach combining artificial neural networks , design of experiments , and genetic algorithms can meet multi-objective models that balance customer and production needs. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based data mining techniques can optimize engineering processes using minimal data, eliminating the need for complex, problem-specific strategies. Moreover, advanced deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks and recurrent neural networks have demonstrated exceptional capabilities in analyzing polymer microstructures and sequential data, uncovering insights that conventional methods often fail to detect. This chapter explores groundbreaking research leveraging AI in polymer extrusion and molding, focusing on enhancing defect-free production, developing advanced materials, optimizing mold design, and improving overall manufacturing efficiency.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, polymer extrusion, and injection molding,

10.1 Introduction

10.1.1 Artificial intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a pivotal research focus in the twenty-first century, impacting a wide range of disciplines such as education, marketing, finance, economics, engineering, science, medicine, business, accounting, the stock market, and law [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Despite its reputation as a contemporary breakthrough, the concept of AI dates to 1955, when Stanford Professor John McCarthy coined the term and described it as “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines” [8]. Since then, AI has evolved dramatically, with machine learning (ML) driving transformative changes in industries, governments, and society [9]. Additionally, AI plays a key role in advancing global sustainability efforts by optimizing energy consumption, logistics, supply chain operations, and waste management. Several branches of AI such as natural language processing, image recognition, ML, and data mining have become foundational to contemporary technological development. With ongoing innovations and increasing global interest, AI continues to be at the forefront of scientific exploration and advancement. Extensive research has been done to develop programs that enable machines demonstrating intelligent behavior, such as playing chess. The current focus in AI is on developing systems that can learn in ways that resemble human learning processes. As a dynamic and continually evolving discipline, AI includes multiple subfields such as ML and deep learning. Central to this is ML, which empowers computers to improve their predictive capabilities and problem-solving skills using algorithms that ultimately aim to replicate elements of human cognitive behavior [10]. Rather than representing a single entity, AI functions as a broad umbrella term, encompassing a diverse and continuously advancing range of modeling capabilities. These capabilities evolve over time, integrating new techniques and methodologies to enhance problem-solving, decision-making, and automation. Figure 10.1 [12] provides a visual depiction of the dynamic evolution of AI, highlighting its ongoing growth driven by progress in ML, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision.

10.1.2 Machine learning

ML is a distinct subset of AI focused on enabling computer systems to enhance their perception, comprehension, decision-making, and actions by learning from experience or data. Unlike traditional programming, which depends on explicitly defined rules and instructions, ML allows computers to autonomously recognize patterns, analyze vast datasets, and make predictions or decisions without direct human intervention. Instead of following predefined logic, ML systems learn from data, adapting their behavior based on observed trends and outcomes. ML is an inherently interdisciplinary field, combining concepts from computer science, statistics, mathematics, psychology, neuroscience, economics, and control theory. By leveraging insights from these diverse areas, it establishes a strong framework for creating intelligent systems that can tackle complex challenges across multiple industries.

At its core, ML is the scientific study of algorithms and statistical techniques that enable computers to perform complex tasks efficiently. By identifying the underlying patterns in data, these models support intelligent, data-informed decision-making processes. Through continuous learning and refinement, ML algorithms enhance their accuracy and efficiency over time. This iterative improvement allows them to adapt to evolving datasets, optimize performance, and foster innovation across diverse fields such as healthcare, finance, autonomous systems, and AI research.

Through iterative learning processes, these models refine their accuracy over time, continuously enhancing performance without direct human intervention. ML techniques are widely applied across industries, from predictive analytics in finance and healthcare diagnostics to speech recognition, autonomous systems, and personalized recommendation engines. With the increasing demand for intelligent automation, ML continues to advance, driving the future of AI-powered innovations. As a distinct field within AI, ML algorithms develop mathematical models from sample data, known as training data, enabling them to make predictions or decisions without requiring explicit programming [12]. Figure 10.2 shows an overview of some of the most accepted ML methods.

The era of explicitly programming machines to solve problems has given way to ML, where computers independently uncover patterns within datasets to generate solutions. By analyzing hidden trends, ML enables predictive insights, allowing for the anticipation and prevention of potential issues before they arise. AI has grown into a diverse and expansive field within computer science, dedicated to creating systems that mimic and enhance human cognitive functions. Intelligent technologies are now capable of executing intricate tasks traditionally dependent on human intelligence, including decision-making, problem-solving, language understanding, pattern recognition, and visual analysis. AI draws from a diverse range of disciplines such as mathematics, data science, neuroscience, and linguistics to create advanced algorithms that learn from data, adapt to new inputs, and progressively enhance their performance. This progression has led to the emergence of core AI domains, such as ML, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision, all of which are instrumental in driving automation, enabling smart decision-making, and solving complex real-world problems.

AI-powered technologies are transforming industries worldwide, spanning sectors such as healthcare, finance, manufacturing, and autonomous systems. From advancing medical diagnostics and fraud detection to driving autonomous vehicles and personalizing virtual assistants, AI is redefining how humans interact with digital environments – boosting efficiency, enhancing precision, and fostering innovation. These intelligent systems perform tasks such as problem-solving, visual recognition, reasoning, decision-making, language processing, and pattern identification. AI utilizes sophisticated algorithms, statistical models, and large datasets to replicate cognitive processes, analyze complex issues, identify hidden patterns, and continuously adapt to new data. With the help of ML, deep learning, and natural language processing, AI is advancing the boundaries of automation and intelligent decision-making. Whether in financial forecasting, self-driving cars, groundbreaking medical innovations, or intelligent digital assistants, AI is reshaping how both businesses and individuals engage with technology and data.

As AI progresses, its capacity to replicate, enhance, and expand human cognitive functions is driving the development of more advanced and adaptive solutions across various industries. Meanwhile, ML stands as a specialized branch of AI, dedicated to empowering computer systems to “learn” from data by identifying patterns and relationships using mathematical models. Instead of depending on explicit programming, ML algorithms employ statistical methods to analyze and interpret data, allowing them to predict outcomes, identify trends, and adjust to new information over time. The principles of ML are strongly grounded in traditional statistical concepts, as depicted in Figure 10.3. ML, often termed “statistical learning” [14, 15], is deeply rooted in statistical principles such as regression analysis, probability theory, and optimization techniques. This strong connection highlights the intersection between classical statistics and modern ML, as both aim to derive meaningful insights from data. ML employs various methodologies tailored to different problem domains, including supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning.

Supervised learning employs labeled datasets to train models, enabling them to predict outcomes based on established input–output relationships. In contrast, unsupervised learning analyzes unlabeled data, revealing hidden structures and patterns without predefined categories. Reinforcement learning takes a distinctive approach, where models improve through a trial-and-error process, earning rewards for optimal actions and facing penalties for suboptimal ones. By integrating these diverse learning methods, ML has transformed industries such as healthcare, finance, automation, and cybersecurity. Its ability to process large datasets, identify complex patterns, and continuously enhance performance has made it fundamental to modern AI applications. Additionally, ML bridges the gap between theoretical statistical principles and real-world decision-making, driving innovation, efficiency, and progress across a range of fields.

10.1.3 Polymer molding and extrusion

The extrusion process traces its origins to the metallurgical industry, with Joseph Bramah patenting the first extrusion method in 1797. His design used a piston-driven mechanism to produce seamless lead pipes. Modern advancements in extrusion technology and machine design have largely resulted from research within the plastics industry. In the food sector, extrusion has been in use since the 1930s and has gained continuous popularity due to its efficiency, consistency, and sustainability [17]. Extrusion has become a fundamental manufacturing process across various industries that require advanced solutions to meet evolving and complex demands. It is particularly crucial in the plastic, food, and pharmaceutical sectors, where precise material processing and consistent product quality are essential. In polymer processing, extrusion involves the use of specialized metal extruders equipped with either single or twin screws, which can operate in a corotating or counterrotating manner. These extruders are designed with highly efficient screw elements that significantly enhance material flow, shear, and mixing. They play a vital role in several key processes, including polymer compounding, the homogeneous blending of fillers and polymers, and facilitating in situ chemical reactions that modify or enhance material properties. The characteristics and performance of extruded polymers are influenced by multiple factors, including screw design, processing conditions, material composition, and temperature control, as illustrated in Figure 10.4. Optimizing these parameters is essential for achieving desired mechanical properties, uniformity, and functionality in the final product. With continuous advancements in extrusion technology, industries can develop high-performance materials tailored to specific applications, ensuring efficiency, sustainability, and innovation in modern manufacturing.

Injection molding is a commonly used method for manufacturing versatile polymer components and structural parts in industries such as automotive, electronics, packaging, and aerospace. The ultimate properties of injection molded products are primarily influenced by factors such as the development of crystalline structures, the distribution and alignment of functional fillers, and the shear and extensional flow fields created during the molding process. Additionally, the cooling phase plays a crucial role in shaping the final characteristics of the manufactured components [19]. A core element of the injection molding system is the injection unit, which is composed of three primary sections: the plasticizing unit, the injection unit, and the pressure maintenance unit. Their functions are as follows:

  1. Plasticizing: The raw material is uniformly melted and plasticized through the combined action of the screw mechanism and heating elements.

  2. Injection: Plastic material in the molten state is injected into the mold cavity at a controlled pressure and speed, facilitated by the movement of the screw.

  3. Pressure maintenance: Once the cavity is filled, the screw remains stationary to counteract shrinkage during cooling, ensuring uniform product quality and preventing material backflow [16].

10.2 Artificial intelligence in polymer extrusion

Advancements in AI – particularly in ML and deep learning – are bringing notable benefits to the polymer extrusion industry. These advanced technologies are playing a key role in solving persistent challenges, enhancing productivity, and fostering innovation. Figure 10.5 highlights how AI can be effectively utilized across different stages of the polymer extrusion process.

Munir et al. [20] demonstrated that AI-driven real-time monitoring systems can significantly improve the control of extrusion processes, particularly in optimizing film thickness. These systems utilize real-time data to adjust parameters, ensuring consistent product quality. By adopting these advanced techniques, manufacturers can significantly reduce defects and minimize material waste during production. In a separate investigation, Munir et al. [21] focused on real-time monitoring of polylactic acid (PLA) degradation during the extrusion process. By leveraging sensor data and machine settings, they developed predictive models to estimate the polymer’s molecular weight and mechanical characteristics. The study found that the combination of recursive feature elimination (RFE) and the random forest (RF) algorithm delivered the highest accuracy, efficiency, and interpretability. Among the key variables influencing PLA degradation and mechanical behavior were pressure and temperature, especially at the extrusion exit. Based on these findings, the researchers recommended the RFE-RF model as a reliable quality control strategy for managing the processing of heat-sensitive polymers like PLA.

Additionally, Çınar et al. [22] examined the application of ML for predictive maintenance within the context of sustainable smart manufacturing, specifically targeting polymer extrusion processes. Their study highlighted the effectiveness of advanced algorithms in analyzing sensor data to identify significant patterns that signal potential equipment failures. By leveraging predictive models, manufacturers can anticipate equipment malfunctions, enabling timely maintenance interventions. This forward-thinking strategy reduces operational expenses, minimizes unplanned downtime, and improves overall efficiency in industrial environments. The integration of ML in manufacturing not only enhances process reliability but also contributes to sustainability by optimizing resource utilization and reducing waste. Abeykoon et al. [23] investigated AI’s potential to reduce energy consumption in extrusion without compromising product quality. Their research provided a detailed analysis of energy usage, pinpointed areas of energy loss, and proposed strategies to improve process efficiency.

AI is also accelerating the development of new polymer formulations and product customization. By predicting the behavior of new materials during extrusion, AI empowers industries such as automotive and aerospace to push the boundaries of high-performance polymers. The technology is transforming the speed and scope of innovation, enabling companies to work faster while fostering greater creativity and flexibility. Park et al. [24] illustrated this impact by applying AI not only to the design of new materials but also to their processing. This is particularly valuable for advanced polymers and composites, which require precise shaping during extrusion and other manufacturing processes.

10.2.1 Optimization in extrusion through artificial intelligence: concepts and use of DAMICORE and FS-OPA

Optimizing polymer processing requires developing a multidimensional model – referred to as the response surface – that maps the relationship between selected input variables and the resulting process outputs. This approach aims to pinpoint the optimal peak or extreme values within this model to maximize efficiency and overall performance. In modern manufacturing, computer simulations play a crucial role in designing polymer processing systems by utilizing mathematical models to replicate and analyze production processes. These simulations allow for precise predictions of process flow by considering factors such as material properties, machine geometry, and operating conditions. For instance, extrusion processes can be assessed based on factors such as flow rate (throughput), pressure and temperature profiles, energy usage, and mixing effectiveness. By utilizing input data, these critical output parameters can be accurately predicted and optimized for improved performance. However, optimizing extrusion is a complex, multi-objective challenge due to the vast number of interrelated parameters, their nonlinear relationships, and conflicting optimization criteria, such as maximizing output while minimizing energy consumption. This complexity makes it difficult to identify a global optimum without getting trapped in local optima [25].

The earliest efforts to optimize the extrusion process using computer simulations were pioneered by Tadmor and Klein [26], who applied regression analysis and response surface methodology to improve screw design through the development of the EXTRUD program [27]. This was followed by Maddock and Smith [28], who showcased extruder design capabilities using computer-generated simulations. Helmy and Parnaby [29] further advanced the field by creating optimization software that employed a steady-state hill-climbing algorithm to enhance melt extruder design. As research progressed, more advanced optimization approaches began to emerge. Potente et al. [30, 31] introduced a screw optimization technique that combined design of experiments with multiple regression, using the REX extrusion model [32, 33, 34]. Likewise, Thibodeau and Lafleur [35, 36] utilized the STATISTICA software to identify optimal response surfaces based on an extrusion model developed at École Polytechnique de Montréal [37, 38]. Wilczyński et al. [39] also adopted statistical methods via the SSEM program [40]. Despite these advances, a major limitation of traditional statistical approaches was the need for a large number of simulations to construct a detailed response surface. This not only increased computational demands but also raised the risk of converging on local optima rather than achieving true global optimization.

The efficiency and overall performance of a single-screw extruder are influenced by a combination of key factors. These include the properties of the processed material – such as its physical, thermal, and rheological characteristics – the geometric design of the system, particularly the screw configuration, and the operational settings, including barrel temperature and screw speed. An extruder’s effectiveness is generally assessed using indicators such as mass throughput, melt temperature, the screw length needed for full material melting, energy consumption, mixing performance, and the extent of viscous heat generation.

To optimize the extrusion process, it is essential to fine-tune screw geometry and operating conditions to maximize output and mixing while minimizing inefficiencies. António Gaspar-Cunha et al. [41] investigated data-driven optimization techniques for single-screw extruders, focusing on multi-objective optimization problems, which require balancing multiple competing factors such as material behavior and screw configurations. Traditionally, these optimization processes rely heavily on expert knowledge; however, data-driven approaches aim to reduce manual intervention by utilizing advanced data analysis and computational methods. By combining data analysis with optimization techniques, the decision-making process becomes more efficient and precise. Data-driven optimization replaces conventional objective function calculations with metamodels or surrogate models that use existing datasets to estimate system behavior. These models enable efficient prediction and optimization of performance metrics. Common techniques include polynomial regression [42], kriging [43], artificial neural networks (ANNs) [44], radial basis function networks [45], and swarm optimization algorithms [46]. AI further enhances this process by allowing computers to independently identify optimal solutions through the analysis of historical data [47]. A variety of AI-based metamodels have been developed for optimization purposes, such as linear and nonlinear regression, incremental dynamic model decomposition [48, 49], support vector machines (SVMs) [50], ANNs [51], decision trees, and the Code2Vect model [52]. However, a significant challenge in applying ML to extrusion lies in the potential impact of unaccounted variables, which can affect the accuracy and generalizability of predictive models. The objective is to leverage the DAMICORE framework, which utilizes distance estimation through compression algorithms known as normalized compression distance (NCD), to aid in investigations where data availability is limited, and external factors may influence the system [53, 54]. Simultaneously, feature sensitivity optimization using phylogram analysis will be utilized to determine the most influential features in real-world scenarios, with a focus on feature interactions and their impact on a specific objective or target [53]. Research has shown that phylogram analysis (OPA) is highly effective in addressing complex combinatorial single- and multi-objective optimization challenges [54, 55]. The FS-OPA approach is built upon the DAMICORE methodology, which facilitates the direct processing of raw data, enables adaptive learning, and generates predictive models for optimization applications.

In practice, the methodology involves storing data for each analyzed object, applying DAMICORE to compute NCD-based distances between data pairs, and generating a distance matrix. Neighbor-joining is then used to construct a phylogram, and finally, feature nodes (FNs) identify clades (or communities). When applied to single-screw extrusion, this approach generates phylograms that provide two levels of learning. The data mining process is designed to analyze and optimize polymer extrusion in a single screw extruder. The dataset utilized for this computational analysis is limited in availability, as it was randomly collected and covers various aspects of the extrusion process, including operational parameters, system geometry, and optimization targets. By implementing the DAMICORE-based learning approach, the study uncovers relationships between decision variables and optimization goals, revealing critical interactions. This analysis provides key insights into the significance of specific design parameters in achieving optimal performance.

10.2.2 Scale-up and optimization for polymer extrusion

xProcess scaling involves adjusting the size of a process according to the defined criteria while striving to preserve critical parameters that mirror those of the original setup. In the context of extrusion scale-up, this means determining the most suitable geometry and operational settings for a larger extruder so that it delivers performance equivalent to that of a smaller, benchmark extruder. This practice is essential in engineering, as it enables the design of industrial-scale extruders using insights gained from laboratory-scale experiments. Over time, various methodologies for extrusion scale-up have been developed and refined. The fundamental principles of this process have been extensively covered in key literature by experts such as Rauwendaal [56], Hensen et al. [57], McKelvey [58], Stevens and Covas [59], Campbell and Spalding [60], and Chen et al. [61]. In addition to these foundational texts, numerous research studies have explored the intricacies of extrusion scale-up. Pearson [62] was the pioneer in performing a thorough and detailed analysis of extrusion scale-up. His study focused on critical aspects of the process, such as the transportation of solids, melting behavior, and the dynamics of melt flow. He determined that successful scale-up could be achieved by maintaining a consistent screw helix angle and barrel temperature, while ensuring that key dimensionless numbers – Graetz, Brinkman, and Nahme – remained constant across different sections of the screw. This method offered several advantages, including balanced solids transport, efficient melting and flow, stable specific energy consumption, and a power–law relationship among the primary scaling factors. Later, Rauwendaal [56, 63] conducted a comparative analysis of various scale-up strategies, uncovering that many resulted in imbalances in solids and melt flow rates or excessive viscous dissipation, thereby highlighting their limitations. Building upon these findings, Covas and Gaspar-Cunha [64] proposed a multi-objective optimization approach for extrusion scale-up, which aimed to identify the best geometry and operating conditions for the target extruder to ensure its key performance metrics closely matched those of the reference extruder. In essence, the objective of the scale-up process is to minimize discrepancies in critical operational parameters between the two machines. Typically, the reference extruder’s specifications are known, and the challenge lies in determining the optimal parameters for the target extruder. This methodology has also been applied to the optimization of both single- and twin-screw extrusion systems [65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, 71, 72]. Implementing this scale-up strategy requires specific steps, as illustrated in Figure 10.6.

Berzin et al. [73] investigated the difficulties involved in scaling up twin-screw reactive extrusion. Their research revealed that conventional scale-up techniques, which depend on diameter ratios, are less effective when complex processes, such as chemical reactions, occur during extrusion. To overcome this challenge, they proposed that mathematical formulas of varying accuracy could be used to estimate critical parameters and identify suitable scaling exponents, resulting in more dependable scale-up guidelines.

10.3 Artificial intelligence in polymer molding: leveraging artificial intelligence for precision injection molding and achieving zero-defect manufacturing

In today’s highly competitive market, maintaining high-quality standards is essential for companies to stand out. Minimizing errors in production processes is crucial, as it leads to lower costs, reduced downtime, and increased overall efficiency. One of the most effective approaches to achieving this is through AI, which has been shown to greatly improve system performance and productivity [74, 75]. Injection molding is an extensively utilized manufacturing method for mass producing polymer components. The primary goal of injection molding is to manufacture consistent, repeatable parts with a uniform appearance. However, the dynamic nature of the process, where parameters continuously fluctuate, can lead to defects, resulting in unexpected costs. Common defects in plastic injection molding (PIM) include unfilled sections, burrs, burn marks, short shots, warping, and flow lines [76, 77]. To mitigate these issues, implementing a monitoring and predictive system that detects defects based on process variations is highly beneficial. An effective and reliable classification system that can identify and alert operators to potential defects is the ideal solution for ensuring quality and minimizing production losses.

Silva et al. [78] developed an advanced intelligent system designed to manage the entire process, from data collection to real-time defect classification. Their approach utilized the European Zero-Defect Manufacturing Platform (ZDMP), which harnesses AI-driven technologies to streamline production workflows and minimize defects. ZDMP operates through a comprehensive framework that incorporates various tools, such as product life cycle assessment, diagnostic and predictive analytics, production control enhancements, quality assurance strategies, and inspection techniques, all aimed at promoting sustainable manufacturing. These tools enable quick process adjustments through both forward and feedback control mechanisms. As part of their work, the researchers proposed an architecture that integrates the RAILES Smart Manufacturing Execution System (MES) with components of the ZDMP platform. RAILES is a state-of-the-art MES that supports real-time monitoring of manufacturing operations. As a next-generation industrial software solution, RAILES provides manufacturers with real-time, data-driven insights to improve decision-making on the production floor. The proposed architecture seeks to seamlessly incorporate RAILES into the ZDMP ecosystem, enhancing its capabilities by utilizing additional features from the ZDMP platform. The general system architecture is depicted in Figure 10.7.

By seamlessly integrating all tools into a unified ecosystem using the RAILES platform and ZDMP, substantial improvements were achieved in shop floor monitoring and operational reliability. This integration led to notable improvements in key performance indicators (KPIs), including a boost of up to 12% in overall equipment effectiveness, a 9% reduction in process downtime, and a significant decline in defective part production. Many researchers have investigated various approaches for quality assurance and defect detection in plastic molding processes. Christian et al. [79] introduced a hybrid methodology that integrates ML techniques with data obtained from both real-world experiments and simulations. Their goal was to improve product quality predictions using limited experimental data to optimize system parameters. However, a key challenge remains in bridging the gap between simulated and experimental data to develop a more effective learning process. Ogorodnyk et al. [80] explored the use of ANN, particularly multilayer perceptron (MLP), in conjunction with decision tree algorithms like J48, to enhance the production process of high-density polyethylene dog bone specimens. However, selecting the most relevant features remained a challenging task. Struchtrup Alexander et al. [81] examined various feature selection techniques, including filter, wrapper, and embedding methods. Their study compared multiple feature sets and evaluated their effectiveness using seven supervised ML algorithms. Although these methods showed promising results, their adoption in industrial settings remains limited, despite the availability of comparable commercial solutions. Park et al. [82] focused on real-time monitoring and control by developing a learning algorithm that adjusts machine input parameters based on sensor data. This proportional correction system was designed to improve the quality of the final product. While traditional quality control methods are available, AI-driven approaches provide substantial benefits over conventional methods, making them a more efficient solution for contemporary manufacturing.

Park et al. [83] developed an advanced system for real-time monitoring, diagnostics, and autonomous quality control in injection molding, aiming to enhance process stability and product consistency. The system gathers vast amounts of data from millions of injection molding cycles using cavity pressure and temperature sensors. Each dataset is assigned a unique cycle ID, linking it to key process parameters, real-time sensor readings, and corresponding product quality classifications. This extensive database allows for in-depth analysis and the creation of reliable reference models. By analyzing the data, the researchers identified correlations between machine input parameters, sensor outputs, and the final product quality. Using these insights, they designed a compensatory algorithm that dynamically adjusts machine input parameters in real time, ensuring optimal processing conditions and consistent product quality. The system continuously compares real-time sensor data with predefined reference values, and when discrepancies are detected, it automatically fine-tunes the process parameters to address any inconsistencies, reducing defects and maintaining uniform quality. This AI-driven approach significantly cuts down on manual adjustments, boosts production efficiency, and improves the overall reliability of injection molding processes. Figure 10.8 illustrates a conceptual flow diagram of the control system’s implementation, which includes two temperature sensors and two pressure sensors placed within the cavity of a car door module. These sensors provide continuous feedback on cavity conditions, enabling precise adjustments to optimize the injection molding process.

Hail Jung et al. [84] conducted a study demonstrating that autoencoder-based models outperform tree-based models in defect classification. Tree-based models are typically built using two main techniques: bagging and boosting. Bagging focuses on effectively organizing the data before building the model, while boosting emphasizes the importance of sensor values and iteratively adjusts residuals to improve the model’s accuracy. As shown in Table 10.1, gradient boosting achieved the highest performance score of 0.7638, indicating that the model correctly classified 76% of defective products. However, only 55% of the predictions identifying products as defective were actually accurate, highlighting a limitation in the model’s precision.

Selvaraj Senthil et al. [85] conducted an extensive review of ML models applied in injection molding machines. Their study explored various factors, including the types of algorithms employed, classifications of AI models, depth layer configurations, training and testing durations, datasets, frameworks, programming languages, user interface designs, and the strengths and weaknesses of each approach. In the realm of ML, supervised learning (Figure 10.9) refers to training a model using labeled input data, allowing it to make highly accurate predictions. This process is like a teacher guiding a student through problem-solving until they achieve precision. Once trained, the model is tested on a separate dataset – typically a subset of the training data in different proportions – to assess its reliability. The approach outlined in [86] yielded the most effective results by precisely predicting the optimal time to replace machine components, thereby reducing damage costs and enhancing operational efficiency. This was accomplished by training the model with multiple supervised learning algorithms and comparing its performance with other research findings. Unsupervised learning (Figure 10.10), on the other hand, is used in scenarios where labeled data is unavailable, requiring the model to identify hidden patterns within the dataset. Without direct supervision, the model autonomously detects similarities and groups related to data points through clustering. This learning process mimics the way humans naturally identify patterns and organize information. The approach outlined in [87] achieved remarkable success by implementing unsupervised cluster analysis for real-time monitoring of mold wear. This method incorporated a sophisticated early warning system designed to detect wear patterns in advance, preventing potential operational failures and improving overall efficiency through proactive maintenance strategies.

Reinforcement learning (Figure 10.11) is a subset of ML in which a system enhances its dataset classification by learning through trial and error. The system receives rewards for correct outputs and penalties for incorrect ones, enabling it to continuously improve its decision-making process. By utilizing this approach, the model learns to optimize task performance by maximizing rewards and minimizing penalties, initially relying on random data trials before progressively improving its accuracy. Shiraishi et al. [88] applied reinforcement learning to predict operating and molding conditions within a short timeframe, achieving efficient molding with reduced power consumption compared to findings from other research studies.

Based on their research, several key conclusions were drawn:

  1. ML algorithms can be effectively applied throughout the injection molding process, from the initial molding stage to the final steps.

  2. Regression equations derived from experimental designs can reduce the need for extensive training datasets in ANNs.

  3. By minimizing repetitive tasks, ML addresses the limitations of simulations, significantly lowering computational power requirements, resource consumption, and processing time. This automation reduces dependence on expert interpretation, facilitating smoother implementation.

  4. The most utilized simulation tools in these studies were MATLAB and C-MOULD.

Ensuring consistent product quality in the PIM process requires the automatic detection of operational defects, which remains a major challenge. Ekta et al. [89] proposed an ML framework aimed at identifying complex faults during PIM. Their approach involved the development of a novel ML-driven gating system (MLGS-PIM), which utilizes ANNs and SVMs to enhance fault detection accuracy and improve overall process reliability. By integrating these two models, the system improves product quality under various conditions. This innovative ML-driven method optimizes the injection molding process by effectively managing simulation data and measurements, while predicting quality characteristics based on multiple parameter values. The study focused on three thermoplastic materials – polystyrene, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) – and employed gating systems with configurations of 3, 4, and 5 gates. The evaluation was based on KPIs such as sum rate, bit error rate, and convergence analysis. The results demonstrated that the proposed MLGS-PIM framework significantly outperformed traditional methods like AntLion optimization and PSO-MSQPA, leading to notable gains in efficiency and accuracy. Figure 10.12 illustrates the MLGS-PIM workflow.

Numerous researchers have explored innovative methods to enhance the accuracy and quality of injection-molded components. Ogorodnyk et al. [90] examined the application of ANN, particularly MLP, in combination with decision tree algorithms such as J48, to develop predictive models aimed at optimizing the production process of high-density polyethylene dog bone specimens. However, a significant challenge in this approach remains the selection of the most relevant features, which is crucial for improving model accuracy and performance. To tackle this challenge, Struchtrup Alexander et al. [91] conducted a comprehensive evaluation of various feature selection techniques, including filter, wrapper, and embedding methods. Their study evaluated the performance of various feature sets by applying seven supervised ML algorithms to derive meaningful insights from the data. While these techniques demonstrated significant potential, their adoption in industrial settings remains limited, despite the increasing accessibility of AI-driven solutions.

Building upon their previous research, Struchtrup Alexander et al. [92] designed a comprehensive framework to automate data preprocessing, enhancing the accuracy of part quality prediction. This framework enhances the analysis of injection molding data by streamlining feature selection and optimizing model performance. By improving the efficiency and reliability of quality assessments, this approach has the potential to facilitate broader integration of ML in manufacturing, ultimately leading to smarter, data-driven production processes.

The choice of ensemble hyperparameters was found to significantly influence overall performance. Despite considerable advancements, fully unlocking AI’s potential in polymer extrusion remains a challenge. A key obstacle is the lack of high-quality, domain-specific datasets required to train AI models effectively. Without robust data, models struggle to generalize across different polymers and extrusion techniques. Another critical issue is the need for interpretable AI models that provide clear justifications for their predictions and decisions. Munir et al. [93] emphasized the critical role of collaboration among materials scientists, data scientists, and engineers in overcoming these challenges. By fostering interdisciplinary cooperation, these efforts can help eliminate obstacles and expedite the seamless integration of AI into polymer extrusion processes.

10.4 Future directions, emerging trends, challenges, and solutions

The foremost challenge in any ML application is determining whether the appropriate data is available, an issue that is particularly significant in extrusion and molding due to the numerous variables involved. Despite these complexities, there is strong optimism about AI’s ability to enhance extrusion efficiency and sustainability, particularly by reducing material waste and energy consumption [94]. Key recommendations include acquiring high-quality data, ensuring model interpretability, and promoting interdisciplinary collaboration [20]. However, certain factors, including ambient temperature, humidity, and the inherent properties of raw materials, are difficult to regulate. These variables, categorized as uncontrollable data, cannot be directly adjusted but significantly influence the process. Recognizing their impact is crucial for developing robust and reliable AI models [95]. The chapter insights take a forward-thinking approach to the future of polymer extrusion and molding, exploring emerging trends and potential breakthroughs that could shape the plastics industry. This underscores the revolutionary role of AI in driving advancements in process optimization, sustainability, and energy efficiency, three critical areas for enhancing polymer extrusion. To guide future advancements, a detailed research roadmap outlines key questions and areas requiring further investigation. By identifying significant gaps and opportunities for innovation, this framework supports the structured and systematic development of AI-driven polymer extrusion, paving the way for continued progress in this evolving field. Future research in AI for polymer extrusion and molding is expected to focus on several key areas:

  • Advanced algorithms and techniques: The continuous advancement of sophisticated ML models, such as deep learning and reinforcement learning, is poised to significantly improve the control of complex extrusion and molding processes while enhancing predictive accuracy. These advanced techniques allow for more precise management of processing parameters, enabling manufacturers to optimize product quality, minimize material waste, and increase overall efficiency. Additionally, emerging generative AI technologies, including generative adversarial networks and variational autoencoders, hold great potential to revolutionize polymer processing. These models can be applied to create innovative polymer material designs with specific properties or to optimize extrusion parameters by simulating different processing scenarios. By leveraging these AI-driven advancements, the industry can achieve greater efficiency, sustainability, and product customization, ushering in a new era of smarter, data-driven manufacturing in polymer extrusion and molding.

  • Real-time data integration and processing: Improving model accuracy and relevance depends on more efficient real-time data collection, integration, and processing. Progress in sensor technologies and data management systems is set to be instrumental in refining these processes, providing more accurate and dependable insights.

  • Scalability and computational efficiency: Overcoming the challenges associated with training and deploying complex ML models is crucial for achieving scalability while maintaining cost efficiency. Future research could focus on developing more efficient computational strategies, such as edge computing and distributed systems, to enhance the performance and feasibility of large-scale execution processes.

  • Adaptability and robustness: Developing ML models that can adapt to evolving process conditions and material characteristics is another critical research direction. Techniques such as transfer learning, meta-learning, and other adaptive methods can enhance model resilience and flexibility in dynamic extrusion environments.

  • Integration with emerging technologies: The integration of ML models with emerging technologies, such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and digital twins, has the potential to transform process optimization and real-time monitoring. This combination fosters greater efficiency, drives innovation, and boosts system performance across a wide range of applications.

In conclusion, integrating artificial learning into polymer extrusion and molding presents substantial opportunities for improving production efficiency and quality control. However, this evolving field requires further research to address existing challenges and unlock new possibilities for optimization. Additionally, as AI becomes more fundamental to manufacturing, it is essential to tackle ethical matters. Critical issues like workforce displacement and data privacy demand proactive strategies to ensure responsible implementation. Implementing strategies for retraining and upskilling displaced workers will be essential to ensure a smooth transition into new roles, fostering a balanced and responsible integration of AI in the industry. Moreover, data security and transparency are essential, necessitating robust protection measures and clear policies on data usage to build trust and ensure responsible AI implementation.

Chapter 11 Discovering new frontiers: material explorations with AI and polymers

Tamanna Rai
Rishabha Malviya

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been a key tool in many fields, including the creation and development of polymer materials, since the start of the digital revolution. This chapter thoroughly analyzes the AI approaches used in this setting, including materials informatics. To explore new horizons in material design and innovation, it focuses on the synergistic integration of AI with polymer science. Additionally, the chapter discusses the application of machine learning (ML) to the development and identification of polymer materials. Lastly, the obstacles and potential for ML future development in polymer materials are suggested.

Keywords: Artificial intelligence, machine learning, polymer science, property prediction, deep learning, smart material, polymer synthesis,

11.1 Introduction

The advancement of machine learning (ML)-based approaches has resulted in the development of cutting-edge methods in scientific fields such as materials science and polymer engineering. ML has recently advanced materials science by utilizing computer algorithms that improve research, awareness, exploration, and modeling [1]. When combined with human ingenuity, these algorithms can greatly aid in the discovery and innovation of new materials for the next innovations [2]. Appropriate design of experiment (DoE) approaches are crucial for the methodical exploration of the design space and the required attributes when designing new materials [3]. This frequently entails choices about a variety of topics, such as system configurations, operating circumstances, and material qualities. The experiential method is used in classical design approaches, which poses some challenges [4]. Primarily, due to their exclusive provision of point-wise evaluation, the relationships between the dependent and independent variables sometimes lack a definitive mathematical representation and are termed “black-box functions” [5]. Secondly, the design space frequently encompasses numerous independent factors, leading to an extensive array of potential combinations. A detailed search rapidly becomes impractical as dimensionality increases [6].

ML seeks to create and evaluate statistical algorithms that acquire knowledge from data and utilize this knowledge on novel, unobserved data, hence enabling independent task performance without direct programming [7]. This advancement functions as a robust instrument for evaluating current polymer materials and identifying novel ones, signifying a substantial transition from conventional methods that depend largely on individual expertise and frequently necessitate considerable time, occasionally extending over decades, from initial experimentation to market introduction [8].

This chapter distinguishes itself by focusing on ML applications in the formulation and optimization of specific polymer classes, addressing unique issues and customized ML methodologies for each. This work distinguishes itself from broader reviews by focusing on the actual application of ML in expediting the design process, forecasting material attributes, and optimizing formulations to attain desired performance more effectively. Moreover, it examines future trends and obstacles, offering a balanced evaluation that considers both current and prospective limitations, a topic often overlooked in the literature [9]. This chapter claims the importance of ML in boosting polymer material innovation by highlighting the shortcomings of traditional experimentation and time-consuming simulations in polymer design [10].

11.2 Fundamental process for machine learning-enhanced polymer development

A genetic algorithm (GA) was employed to construct numerous polymer networks with specified attributes [11]. Subsequently, ML techniques were applied to calculate the characteristics of polymers and conduct design studies. These models pertain to property prediction or new material discovery and follow the subsequent procedures, as shown in Figure 11.1.

  • Stage 1: Acquiring molecular structures from literature or accessible databases.

  • Stage 2: Molecules are fingerprinted into shapes that computers can recognize. To be more specific, this involves turning these three-dimensional chemical shapes into tensors.

  • Stage 3: Researchers can develop a structure-property prediction algorithm by selecting an appropriate ML framework and entering molecular data.

  • Stage 4: Selecting a suitable ML model to build novel compounds and using the framework to predict features in Stages 1–3.

  • Stage 5: Examining these new compounds using domain expertise to confirm that the selected samples adhere to essential chemical principles and can be synthesized. Ultimately, one can acquire the requisite polymer [12, 13, 14, 15].

11.3 Data collection

Data is crucial when using ML to research polymer membranes. The efficacy of ML models is greatly impacted by their accuracy and the volume of data used to train them [16]. One of the most significant obstacles in constructing strong ML models is the limited availability of data, particularly in terms of maintaining superior quality [17]. Inadequate, low-quality datasets do not accurately reflect the complete diversity of the overall data population, potentially leading to biased forecasts. Training with limited datasets frequently leads to overfitting; thus, the model captures noise instead of the expected basic patterns. As a result, it loses its ability to extrapolate to new, unknown facts [18]. By reducing bias, improving feature representation, and giving models more ability to make predictions across the training data, large, exceptional datasets can help mitigate these disadvantages [19]. The absence of clearly defined criteria for identifying low-quality data complicates the assessment of data trustworthiness. Verifying the data can enhance the dataset’s quality by detecting outliers or inaccurate data points [20].

Making sure that the dataset contains at least ten times as many data points as there are input variable types is a widely used strategy to avoid overfitting and improve model dependability. The following subsections outline common data collection methods [21].

11.3.1 The compilation of datasets from literature

The comprehensive global citation database “Web of Science” contains about one million papers related to the term “polymer” [22]. Furthermore, given that polymer research is an expeditiously advancing discipline, the quantity of accessible polymers will perpetually increase [23]. This technique has been accepted by a multiplicity of academics since it alleviates the restrictions of the current information system and allows researchers to engineer particular polymers [24]. The drawback of this strategy is that dataset creation is labor-intensive, and the data points may be fewer than those from existing databases [25]. Recently, researchers developed a mechanical data extraction approach based on language processing algorithms and ML. This could be an excellent technique to avoid the challenges associated with gathering datasets based on books [26]. The fact that almost all research studies only report selected findings, meaning that only partial information is available, is another issue with this data collection process [27]. Consequently, these data do not conform to the Gaussian distribution criteria and may lead to overfitting in ML models.

11.3.2 Compilation of data from theoretical models or scientific computations

Academics frequently utilize scientific computational techniques or conceptual frameworks when they cannot locate the necessary details in current databases or publications [28]. For example, Liu and Cao derived 11 pertinent parameters to predict glass transition temperature using density functional theory (DFT). Using a molecular dynamics (MD) model and ML, Zhu et al. created 300 different kinds of single-chain polymer compounds with high heat conductivity. Using the ADAPT toolkit, researchers identified 100–300 relevant parameters for employing ML to predict the temperature at which glass transitions [29].

11.3.3 Data preprocessing and feature engineering

After being collected, the initial information needs to be cleaned up and set up before it can be used in ML models or for more research. A lot of things go into preprocessing or the preparation of data. Data cleaning includes finding and fixing mistakes, getting rid of duplicates, and getting rid of outliers from a set of data [30]. This is done to make sure that the data is accurate and of higher quality, and that there are no flaws. Adding new numbers to a set of data to fill in missing ones is called data imputation [31]. Data retrieved from the literature frequently contains datasets with missing values for specific variables, necessitating this procedure. Due to its intrinsic chemical and physical properties, raw data is sometimes used by researchers, while others opt to use mean or median values for data calculation [32]. Data normalization is the process of changing the distribution of data so that it is suitable for ML analysis. This means changing the data to fit a normal distribution and normalizing it to have a standard deviation of one and a median of zero [33]. It is essential to translate categorical features into a format that is interpretable by computers, as ML models generally cannot directly analyze categorical data (e.g., types of solutes, polymers, or solvents). Examples of these computer-readable formats include one-hot encoding, label encoding, and binary encoding [34].

11.4 Fingerprinting

During this stage, scientists transform 3D molecules into scalars or tensors, facilitating computer interpretation and subsequent processing. We acknowledge that several fingerprinting methodologies are discussed separately below [35].

11.4.1 Line notation

The Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) is a commonly utilized format for depicting molecular structures [36]. SMILES strings comprise alphanumeric characters that denote bonds and atoms within a molecule [37]. They contain information about the molecule’s atoms, linkages, rings, and branches. SMILES strings are notable for their direct usefulness as descriptors in ML models and their capacity to be transformed into alternative descriptors [38]. As a result, SMILES strings are crucial for molecular expression in a way that ML algorithms can understand which streamlines the application of ML to the creation of polymers.

11.4.2 Morgan fingerprinting

Rogers and Hahn developed Morgan fingerprinting as a re-execution of the extended connectivity fingerprint (ECEP). Each monomer can have its distinct sequential atom numbering obtained using this method. Three essential steps make up this method. First, each atom in the monomer is assigned an integer value. Second, the unique identification number of each atom is updated to match that of its neighbors (see Figure 11.2) [39]. In this method, each repeat generates an identifier that represents progressively bigger spherical components encircling the central atom. Third, to generate a single representative, identical attributes are eliminated [40]. Morgan fingerprinting may be a more effective approach to display 3D structure than linear notation encoding since it can describe each atom and its neighbors. This strategy was also employed in numerous investigations. To put it into practice, use the open-source cheminformatics software RDKit [41].

11.5 Machine learning algorithm

The ML approach aims to establish a connection between the fingerprinted input and the target property, which is an effective substitute for predicting the target feature [42]. Currently, the model is constructed using both linear and nonlinear regression techniques. The most widely used techniques are kernel-based regression and artificial neural networks (ANNs). Below is a brief description of various techniques [43].

11.5.1 Regression model and nonlinear regression algorithms

The linear regression algorithm was one of the original and most basic approaches, representing the desired characteristic as a linear function using fingerprints. These models fail to adjust for the nonlinear relationship between descriptions and qualities, limiting their predictive effectiveness [44]. The so-called “Kern trick” is often used to solve this problem in complex regressions. Kernel functions, such as polynomial kernels and radial basis functions, translate data into a higher-dimensional feature space. In linear regression, this is used in place of the original fingerprint x [45]. In the original feature space, this process leads to a nonlinear regression. Some kernel-based methods that have been used are Gaussian process regression (GPR), support vector machine (SVM) and kernel ridge regression (KRR) [46]. For example, KRR has been used to predict the features of polymers using extensive DFT calculations [47]. To expedite the search for high-quality polymers and determine their dielectric constant at various frequencies, particle swarm optimization (PSO) and interval support vector regression were suggested by Yin et al. This study uses the PSO method to enhance the SVM hyper-parameters [48].

11.5.2 Random forests

This approach skillfully handles the complex interaction of attributes by combining a variety of decision trees. The maximum allowable depth for all trees and the total number of trees in the forest were two important factors that were adjusted to enhance their performance [49].

11.5.3 Gradient boosting machines (GBMs)

Methods like LightGBM and XGBoost were applied to improve prediction accuracy. These models are resistant to overfitting and able to handle large datasets, as they repair faults from earlier rounds [50].

11.5.4 Graph convolutional neural network

As previously mentioned, molecular graphs can only use graph convolutional neural network (GCNN) to predict properties. Convolution and pooling are the two ways that GCNN differs from CNN [51]. The GCNN kernel is impacted by its surroundings, whereas the CNN kernel has a standard 2D receptive field and moves at a regular Euclidean distance. Second, CNN polls uniformly in a 2D grid, but GCNN polls no uniformly in its surroundings [52]. Complex network connection in polymer graphs is an example of a strange area that GCNN can handle because it has two unique properties. A study that employed GCNN to identify the locations of interactions between protein kinase inhibitors found that the accuracy was 86% (Wang et al., 2015) [53]. When Tao et al. utilized GCNN to predict a photopolymer’s glass transition temperature; their model was accurate up to 79.18% of the time [54]. Altae-Tran et al. employed GCNN in their study to accomplish one-shot acquiring knowledge, and their model performs well in small molecule prediction [55]. When Aldephi et al. used the modified GCNN, they looked at the link after polymerization and came up with a new network called wD-MPNN, which seemed to work better than the old GCNN [56].

11.5.5 The ANN and the deep neural network

Many years of work have gone into making ANN and deep neural networks (CNN) that work like the brain to learn the connections between different traits and descriptions by doing things over and over again. The output layer displays how well the potential polymers function, while the hidden layers demonstrate the connections between the input and output layers [57]. To extract significant features from the input layer and further simplify the features, CNN adds additional standard and pool layers. The convolutional layers are made up of trainable filters that perform distinct convolutions across the entire input. This allows local characteristics to be extracted [58]. Pooling layers further reduce feature dimensions by pooling sub regions into a single result. Maximum pooling is the most prevalent type of pooling. When compared to completely linked layers, conventional and pool layers have significantly less buried neurons. This allows networks to go much deeper [59]. ML models for the appropriate choice of thermal conductivity, glass transmission temperature, and polymer solvent pairings were created using NNs. A binary classification neural network (NN) model that can determine whether a solvent is suitable for a polymer or not was trained using 11,958 pairs of polymers and good solvents and 8,469 pairs of polymers and nonsolvents to identify the best polymer-solvent pairs. To forecast how thermally conductive polymers will be, we used a CNN trained on thermal conductivities found by traditional MD models. Wei et al. developed a CNN model using 2D cross-sectional photos of polymer composites, which has been shown to accurately forecast how well materials transport heat [60].

11.5.6 Decision tree

To help in decision-making, decision trees employ a framework similar to a tree to foretell potential outcomes. It has also been widely utilized for polymer discovery because to its easy understanding ability and reliance on graphical depiction [61]. Information gain, gradient boosting, and a variety of other methods have been used to construct decision trees. Li et al. predicted how hydrogels self-assemble using logistic regression, decision trees, and gradient boosting, which may be useful in biomedical settings like cell culture [62]. Bhowmik et al. utilized decision trees and principal component analysis (PCA) to predict the specific heat of polymers [63]. Kumar et al. separated ribonucleoprotein absorption, toxicity, and editing rates into high and low groups using random forest [64].

11.5.7 Variational autoencoders (VAEs)

We looked into the hidden space of polymer structures to come up with different design choices. VAEs used a probabilistic approach to model complex distributions and come up with new polymer options that met certain criteria [65].

11.6 Polymer design algorithms

Upon completion of training, the polymer replacement models can be employed to accelerate the discovery of novel polymers. Here are two distinct approaches. The first approach employs predictions to identify candidates that meet specific property requirements. In contrast, the second approach uses generative and genetic models to directly produce desirable candidates [66].

11.6.1 Enumeration

Artificial intelligence methodologies are frequently employed to expedite the systematic design and advancement of innovative materials. These technologies operate by effectively exploring a designated chemical area [67]. The ML models we’ve already talked about are used to guess the properties of a big group of possible polymers that are listed according to a physical or chemical scheme. The process of reducing the list according to specific screening criteria comes next [68]. In the end, a ranked list of qualified candidates for the objective application is eventually generated. The first possibilities could be synthetic polymers that have already been made, or they could be hypothetical polymers that have been made by humans or machines, showing the trends in a way that looks like “Ashby plots” of different ML-predicted features for tens of thousands of known or synthesizable polymers [69]. It is possible to choose different combinations of properties based on the needs of specific use [70]. For example, polymers with a high glass transition temperature, a high dielectric constant, and a big band gap can withstand temperature extremes. However, the polymeric electrolytes used in Li-ion batteries must have the proper band gap, electron affinity, and ionization energy. Conversely, gas permeability and selection must be precisely calibrated for polymer membranes [71].

11.6.2 Evolutionary strategy (genetic algorithm GA)

One term for GA’s underlying principle is “natural selection.” It is simple to treat polymers with GA due to their inherent structure. Polymers consist of several chemical units that are covalently bound to one another. The characteristics of a polymer’s chemical components determine the material’s final characteristics [72]. To find new potential polymers with the desired characteristics, the GA method employs a sequence of crossover, mutation, and selection procedures [73]. To begin, a large number of polymers are generated at random from a pool of monomers using procedures such as crossover, pruning, mixing, and mutation, which alter the chemical building blocks of the monomers. This process is repeated until a significant number of progeny polymers are obtained [74]. The top candidates for the next generation of polymers are chosen based on a user-defined objective score that takes into account their ideal features. This GA cycle is repeated until a sufficient number of candidates possessing the necessary attributes are identified [75]. GA has been used for more than just finding polymers. It has also been applied to solve problems in materials science, such as uncovering hidden links between material properties and creating functional forms of interatomic potentials. The objective function being evaluated during the selection step is an important part of the GA design scheme. This step has been a big problem for finding new polymers because figuring out properties through tests or calculations is very expensive and takes a long time. However, new, cost-effective, and accurate polymer property models have made this feasible [76]. It is now possible to compute the target function in a fraction of a second. This advancement enables the GA approach to go well beyond preestablished candidate sets and genuinely investigate a very rich chemical polymer space. Additionally, polymers that concurrently meet several property criteria might be targeted by establishing a property-weighted goal function [77].

11.7 Application

11.7.1 Polymer electrolytes design for Li-ion batteries

Rechargeable Li-ion batteries are now commonly employed in a variety of industries, including microelectronics and airplanes. Increasingly, people are interested in developing new, superior solid polymer electrolyte materials because they are required in industry [78]. For Li-ion batteries to perform at their best, the polymer solutions should exhibit high ionic conductivity, high Li-ion transference, a low glass transition temperature, and a wide electrochemical stability window. Experiments to identify the best electrolytes take a lot of time, so data-driven aided polymer design methods are a great way to save time [79]. For instance, to assist with coarse-grained MD simulations, Wang et al. used ML to develop novel polymer solutions with strong ionic conductivity [80].

11.7.2 Rational design of polymer dielectrics

The ability of a polymer to polarize in an electric field is determined by its dielectric constant. For electronics, both extremely high and low dielectric constant polymers are required [81]. In an integrated circuit (IC), low dielectric polymers are used as insulation to keep signal-carrying wires apart and to prevent coupling between metal lines that are close to one another [82]. Conversely, high dielectric polymers are essential for semiconductors and high-density energy storage devices. Many well-known polymers have a low dielectric constant and are frequently used to prevent objects from coming into contact with one another. However, achieving high dielectric constants in plastic materials remains challenging [83]. Several recent initiatives have employed data-driven approaches to develop high dielectric polymers.

11.7.3 Polymer membrane design for gas separation

Polymers are also excellent choices for gas separation due to their enormous surface area [84]. Since the early 1990s, people have been particularly interested in a class of polymers known as polymers of intrinsic microporosity [84]. Researchers must investigate the creation of new polymeric membranes because the existing ones have poor selectivity and degrade over time [85]. It’s not easy, though, to come up with polymer membranes that work well and let a lot of gas through while also being selective. Some early research has been conducted to accelerate the search for polymer membranes using data-driven methodologies. For example, gas permeability prediction models have been developed, and the enumeration approach has been utilized to identify polymer membrane candidates for separating CO2 and CH4 [86].

11.7.4 Inverse design of thermally conductive polymers

Due to their versatility and ease of manipulation, polymers are increasingly being used as materials for semiconductors, energy storage devices, and several micro/nano fluidics devices. The long-term stability, sustainability, and durability of these devices depend on their ability to effectively dissipate heat. This is because they generate significant heat during operation. The naturally low heat conductivity of polymers needs to be raised so that they can be used successfully in the above-mentioned situations [87]. To comprehend and control the thermal conductivity of polymeric materials, a great deal of research has been conducted. These studies demonstrate that polymer conductivity is intimately related to how they are structured, what chemicals they contain, how they interact with other chemicals, and a variety of other environmental conditions and industrial conditions [88]. These intricate relationships offer thermally conductive polymers a wide range of design options.

11.7.5 Conducting polymer design for electronic applications

Polymers usually don’t conduct electricity, but some of them do. These intrinsically conducting polymers are used in electronics such as field-effect transistors, light-emitting diodes, and organic solar cells [89]. Molecular doping is often used to make polymers even more conductive, but it takes longer to find the best pairs of polymers and dopants that work well together. This is because the working conditions, how the dopants and polymers interact, and how the electrons move are all very complicated [90]. Polymer informatics can improve this process by developing models that predict conductivity and utilizing iterative methods to identify the best polymer-dopant pairs. It is supported by the fact that random forest and enhanced regression trees were used to find many good donor/acceptor pairs for organic solar cells [91].

11.8 Future research directions

The promise of artificial intelligence and ML in polymer science is not without its obstacles, which must be overcome before the field can fully benefit from these technologies.

11.8.1 Data quality and quantity

Dataset growth and improvement should be the researchers’ priority. This method allows for the collection of a vast amount of high-resolution experimental data, which significantly improves model training and validation.

11.8.2 Algorithm development

It is important to keep coming up with new methods and techniques, especially for dealing with problems that keep coming up, like overfitting, generalization, and processing efficiency. ML techniques that are mixed in hybrid models may also be a good way to boost speed.

11.8.3 Computational resources

Training and using cutting-edge ML models require a lot of work.

11.9 Conclusion

In conclusion, the combination of AI and ML with polymer science has opened up fresh opportunities for material exploration. Researchers can use ML algorithms to quickly screen and optimize polymer qualities, accelerating the development of new materials. AI can predict the behavior of polymers at various stages, including monomer selection, polymerization, and the polymer’s final properties. This enables the development of polymers with customized characteristics for specific purposes.

The combination of polymers and AI has far-reaching implications for a variety of areas. For example, the design of polymer membranes for gas separation, polymer electrolytes for lithium-ion batteries, and rational polymer dielectrics. Furthermore, AI can help create polymers for energy storage devices such as super capacitors and batteries. We may expect the development of breakthrough polymer-based goods that will improve many aspects of our lives as long as research in this area continues. Finally, the combination of AI and polymers has the potential to transform material science and other domains.
