Chapter 14 Robotics innovations in nanotechnology: redefining polymer science with AI

Komal Gupta
Niranjan Kaushik
Amit Singh
Vikram Sharma
Tanya Biswas

Abstract

Artificial intelligence (AI), nanotechnology, and robotics are integrating to transform polymer science and open up previously unattainable opportunities for improved functionalization at the nanoscale and material innovation. This chapter examines how AI-driven robotics is revolutionizing the generation of specialized nanomaterials, with an emphasis on the synthesis, properties, and uses of polymers. Researchers can speed up discovery processes, anticipate molecular behavior, and optimize polymer design by combining robotic equipment and machine learning algorithms. This minimizes time-to-market for novel materials. AI also makes it possible for robotic platforms to regulate atoms with great accuracy, which makes it possible to synthesize polymers with improved mechanical, electrical, and thermal properties.

The chapter elaborates the challenges and future prospects of this comprehensive subject while exhibiting modern advancements in AI-assisted robotics such as autonomous material testing and self-assembling polymer systems. In addition to advancing the field of nanotechnology, the ability to change a variety of industries, constituting electronics, healthcare, and environmental sustainability is shown by such collaborative approach.

Keywords: Nanotechnology, robotics, algorithms, sustainability, healthcare,

14.1 Introduction

Integrating nanotechnology and artificial intelligence (AI) has become an emerging field with revolutionary promise in the rapidly evolving environment of contemporary innovation and technology [1]. Together, these two fields – each revolutionary in its own right – have the potential to expand human potential and make possible innovations that were previously only found in fictional realms. Nanotechnology and AI together mark a significant advancement in exploration of technological and scientific discovery. This is crucial to identify the history of both nanotechnology and AI and comprehend how each has influenced the modern world separately in order to fully grasp the significance of this convergence.

Originating in the middle of the twentieth century, AI is frequently considered the apex of science and machine learning (ML) [2]. The goal of early AI research was to imitate human cognitive processes through expert systems and symbolic reasoning. However, a lack of computing power and irrational expectations caused the industry to experience multiple “AI winters.” Three main elements have contributed to the rebirth of AI in recent decades: computational power, big data, and algorithmic innovation [3, 4]. AI algorithms now have a wealth of training data thanks to the surge in data generation brought about by the digital age. This resulted in the research of technical methods, especially deep learning, which fueled advances in reinforcement learning (RL), processing of natural language, and picture identification [5, 6]. The learning and implementation of models of AI were greatly hastened by hardware advancements such as graphics processing units and AI chips, which made formerly difficult jobs possible [7]. Recurrent neural networks and convolutional neural networks (CNNs), two more modern AI algorithms created by researchers, are particularly good at picture and speech recognition. AI is now pervasive in many aspects of our daily life, from driverless cars to predictive systems of healthcare. It keeps developing quickly and expanding its powers into new areas.

On the other hand, the multidisciplinary discipline of nanotechnology arose from the discovery that matter had special characteristics at the nanoscale, which is often described as structures with dimensions less than 100 nanometers [8]. The foundation for nanotechnology was established by Richard Feynman’s seminal 1959 talk, “There’s plenty of space at Bottom,” which visualized the modification of atoms and molecules [9]. Since then, nanotechnology has advanced significantly, making it possible to design and produce nanomaterials and nanodevices with remarkable qualities [10, 11]. Nanomaterials with specific properties, such as carbon nanotubes (CNTs), quantum dots, and graphene, have been created by scientists and engineers, creating new opportunities in materials science, electronics, and energy storage. Scientists are producing nanoscale machines and robots for use in everything, from ecological restoration to medication delivery [12, 13].

Because AI and nanotechnology have complementary strengths, their convergence is a logical development. The accuracy of nanotechnology at the atomic and molecular level complements AI’s data processing skills and capacity to manage intricate algorithms [14]. This convergence presents special difficulties that demand careful investigation, but it also offers huge potential in a number of areas, for example, materials research, healthcare, and environment monitoring. Interaction of both AI and nanotechnology offers novel details to some important worldwide problems as both domains develop further, bringing in a new era of creativity (Figure 14.1). Scientists and society at large must comprehend this synergy and its consequences.

This chapter attempts to address these issues head-on through offering a thorough examination of the state of AI in nanotechnology today, pointing out important knowledge gaps and providing perspectives into the collaborative, ethical, and regulatory aspects of the developing area. Through resolving numerous problems, the chapter aims to widen the door for more ethical and informed introduction of nanotechnology and AI into the rapidly developing technical framework. This chapter’s rationale is the understanding that both AI and nanotechnology have already significantly impacted society on their own. AI has impacted various fields such as manufacturing, transportation, and finance, thanks to the potential to carry enormous data and complex functions with high precision [15, 16].

However, nanotechnology has rendered it possible to engineer and modify materials at the nanoscale levels, offering a world where matter’s properties behave differently than they do at the macroscopic level [17]. However, the potential for previously unknown breakthroughs that might transform entire industries and resolve crucial global issues lies at the intersection of these domains. Recognizing how AI can be used in nanotechnology is not just a theoretical pursuit but also a practical necessity. The speed in the discovery of new materials is enhanced; it has modified nanoscale manufacturing techniques, improved medical care, and helped create sustainable energy sources. A methodical investigation is necessary to completely understand these possibilities and negotiate the complexity of this progress. In order to increase awareness and encourage responsible innovation, it explores and outlines the moral, legal, and societal issues brought about by AI and nanotechnology collectively. In order to completely identify the idea of this convergence, the chapter highlights the significance of cooperation between domain-specific specialists, nanotechnologists, and AI researchers. The evaluation offers suggestions and information that can direct upcoming studies and educate decision-makers about the ethical advancement and application of AI in nanotechnology.

14.2 Robotics

The field of robotics incorporates a number of engineering and technology disciplines such as electronics, material science, mechanical engineering, and bioinformatics. All engineering branches and their technologies must coordinate for manufacture and operation. Applications of robots range from basic manufacturing to the military and defense industries. Diverse applications necessitate distinct operational methodologies and component kinds. Typically, all robots need to be strong, flexible, and long-lasting. They must also be lightweight for some applications, such as biological fields. These characteristics cause polymers, a large class of materials that compose of thermoplastics, nanomaterials, elastomers, etc., to function. The ability to modify polymers to achieve desired properties is one of its characteristics.The function of various polymers in the domain of robotics is briefly discussed in this chapter. Robotics is the branch of science that studies how to design, build, operate, and use robots. Robotics additionally encompasses the design and operation of the technological devices that control them. In his 1920 play, Rassum’s Universal Robots, Czech novelist Karel Capek used the term “robot” for the first time. The Czech word for worker or servant is where the word “robot” first appeared. Robots are defined by the Oxford Dictionary as “machine capable of performing complex sequence of actions automatically, particularly those which can be programmed by a human.”

14.3 Role of polymers in robotics

Robots are used in the polymers composition, and polymers and plastics are important components of robot manufacturing. Packaging, polymer manufacture, and other industries use commercial and industrial robots. Most of the time, polymers are inexpensive, lightweight, pliable, flexible, and simple to make. Because of these characteristics, they can be incorporated in numerous industries, for example, electronics, aerospace, and home products. Polymers can be molded into any shape, and their characteristics can be altered to suit the application. Compared to traditional robots, soft robotics are preferred these days due to their ease of contact with humans.

The most common polymer types used in robotic applications include thermoplastics, elastomers, polymeric gels, and materials based on epoxy and acrylic [18].

14.4 Advancements in nanotechnology

Molecular- and atomic-level engineering manipulation of valuable materials and devices is the focus of nanotechnology. Compared to existing developments in the chemical, biological, electronic, and related sectors, the development of nanotechnologies offers new and improved materials and devices that offer substantially higher overall performance, dependability, and efficiency.

Applications such as molecular electronics, tumors in which nanodevices can differentiate between cancerous and noncancerous ones and electro-mechanical computing devices are crucial for the advancement of whole new fields of research and technology. The gradual reduction of material size is a major benefit of materials science in nanotechnology. The primary benefit of precision nanodevices, which have been developed, is the unmatched precision they can attain.

However, other significant features of molecular interactions in related biological systems must be addressed in the development of nanodevices, as many of their operational characteristics are derived from molecular interactions between nanodevices, during use. The combination of computational and physical components is the other significant obstacle still facing nanodevices. Let’s conclude by pointing out that a key component of contemporary advanced materials research is the process of assessing the quality of functional materials at microscopic to nanoscopic levels [19].

14.4.1 Nanomanufacturing and quality control

A paradigm change in nanomanufacturing and quality control is being driven by the combination of AI and nanotechnology [20, 21]. AI’s incorporation into nanomanufacturing procedures has rendered it easier for scientists to precisely and efficiently assemble nanoscale structures, which is resulting in revolutionary advances across a range of industries: manufacturing processes are being revolutionized by AI-controlled robots with nanoscale precision [22, 23].

These robots’ unmatched precision in manipulating nanomaterials makes it possible to assemble complex structures that were previously difficult to create. 3D nanoprinting methods are being optimized by AI algorithms. This approach opens up new possibilities in materials science, electronics, and medical devices by precisely creating intricate nanoscale architectures [24, 25]. Custom-designed nanomaterials and components are becoming possible thanks to AI-driven nanoscale additive manufacturing technologies [26]. This strategy has broad consequences for areas like aerospace, where there is a need for strong, lightweight nanomaterials (Figure 14.1).

AI plays an essential role in quality control, guaranteeing that devices and nanomaterials fulfill high requirements of dependability and efficiency [27, 28]. Machine vision systems driven by AI can examine materials and structures at the nanoscale with remarkable precision [29]. By identifying flaws and variations that the human eye might miss, these technologies improve the quality of the final product [30]. Real-time quality feedback is provided by AI-driven sensors and monitoring devices integrated into nanomanufacturing machinery [31]. This feature makes it possible to modify manufacturing procedures instantly, which reduces waste and mistakes. AI predicts maintenance requirements by analyzing data from nanomanufacturing equipment [32]. AI-driven preventative maintenance reduces downtime and guarantees constant production quality [33].

AI is used to optimize nanomanufacturing operations because of its ability to access huge data in order to determine the ideal factors for manufacturing of materials and guarantee high-grade nanomaterials, low consumption of resources, examine data from manufacturing processes [34, 35]. AI-enhanced materials characterization methods shed light on nanomaterial characteristics. This data guides modifications to production procedures, resulting in materials with the required qualities.

14.4.2 Nanotechnology for biomedical soft robots

Since its introduction twenty years ago, soft robots have gained a lot of research interest; the biomedical field has been regarded as a crucial area of application [36]. Soft robots with promising features have been made possible by recent advancements in functional materials, particularly improved soft substances, which have significantly increased their prospective uses in the biomedical arena. Soft robots are divided into in vitro and in vivo categories on the basis of biomedical application characteristics. To help with difficult biomedical procedures and the replacement of human body parts with artificial organs, soft robots of in vivo category – that is, robots that are integrated with the human body [37] – are created [38]. For instance, research has been done on using soft robots to perform endoscopic procedures and minimally invasive surgery on humans, as well as to deliver medications under the skin or inside blood vessels. Conversely, soft robots of in vitro category – that is, robots that are cooperated outside the human body – evolved for a variety of biomedical procedures, ranging from precise surgery to physical rehabilitation. For instance, it has been stated that biomedical soft robots can help patients with rehabilitation by physically supporting them [39]. Biocompatibility is crucial in the design and construction of biomedical soft robotics because of the unique application conditions found in the human body. Specifically, to provide full functionality and good acceptability in application scenarios, the materials used in biomedical soft robots must entirely be compatible with organs and tissues [40].

14.4.3 Nanorobotics and medicine

Innovative developments in healthcare are being made possible by the intersection of nanorobotics and medicine. This convergence addresses medical issues in diagnosis, therapy, and medication distribution by utilizing the accuracy and versatility of nanoscale robots in the direction of AI algorithms [41]. The application of nanorobotics in medicine has enormous promise for diagnosis. These microrobots, which are frequently made to resemble biological objects, are extremely good at navigating the human body [42]. They can have sensors installed for cellular or molecular diagnostics and real-time monitoring. For instance, early detection and intervention may be made possible by the nanorobots’ ability to identify infections, cancer cells, or disease-related biomarkers, strong classification performance, and reasoning. A neuroscience-inspired method called the complementary learning fuzzy neural network, suggested as computer-assisted intervention tool, is employed to analyze thermograms because of its superior classification performance, human-like reasoning, and high preliminary screening accuracy when compared to manual diagnostics [43]. Drug distribution is among the most exciting uses of nanorobotics in medicine. By avoiding healthy tissues and reducing adverse effects, these nanoscale robots can deliver medications straight to their intended locations [44]. Nanorobots that are guided by AI algorithms are able to traverse intricate biological settings and get past obstacles like the blood–brain barrier. By lowering the necessary drug dosage and improving therapeutic efficacy, this targeted drug delivery strategy minimizes toxicity and side effects. Additionally, minimally invasive surgery is being revolutionized by AI-driven nanorobotics. These robots have remarkable precision in executing complex tasks. Advanced sensors are responsible for the high precision of nanorobots, which influences their capacity to navigate the complex biological environment.

AI and nanorobotics together enhance autonomy and decision-making [45]. These nanorobots are able to make effective choices in response to shifting bodily situations by using real-time data from sensors. For instance, they can react rapidly to emergencies or modify medicine release rates in accordance with the patient’s physiological parameters. By increasing the accuracy of targeted medicines, better diagnostics, and creative treatment approaches, the future of medicine is expected to see significant breakthroughs due to the combination of nanorobotics and AI. By utilizing modes of hybrid control such as light field trigger and magnetic field drive, bioactive microbots can execute targeted treatments like tumor removal with minimal or no adverse effects. AI integration has the potential to further optimize nanorobots, enabling a response to intricate biological circumstances that could basically revolutionize patient outcomes and clinical practice [46]. One of these is the advancement of personalized medicine techniques, in which nanorobots are customized to an individual’s genes and medical requirements. Furthermore, AI-powered nanorobotics have the potential to transform regenerative medicine by repairing damaged organs or tissues at the cellular level [47].

14.4.4 Nanotechnology in biorobotics

The field of biorobotics is widely transdisciplinary in both science and technology. In order to improve our understanding of human physiology, the initial definitions from mid-1990s emphasized challenges of simulating and modeling biological systems [48]. Biological systems and robotics were conceptually related and viewed as “metaphor” in this viewpoint. It was also seen as an essential connection between AI-based technology and individuals.

The following are the main goals of biorobotics: (1) establishing skilled mechanical systems with improved functionality and performance; (2) using robotic materials to better understand specific animal (including human) mechanisms and behaviors; and (3) achieving safe and efficient interactions (like new low invasive therapies) with biological structures. Nowadays, nanotechnology is significant for achieving these objectives, providing previously unattainable possibilities [49].

Particularly for medical applications, nanorobots are regarded as one of the most promising systems. Nanorobots are intelligent systems composed of nanoscale component assemblies through overall dimensions below the range of micrometers [50]. Although it is generally acknowledged that medical nanorobots with true functionality will significantly improve healthcare, a number of problems must be resolved before the many functional components that constitute a nanorobot can be effectively developed and assembled. The physical principles that govern interactions at the nanoscale level are primarily responsible for these challenges. In addition to the significant scaling of effects of volume (related to weight, heat capacity, and inertia) that are superimposed by surface effects (related to forces of adhesion, heat transfer, and friction), chemical bonding forces play a larger character by decreasing the size, as do quantum effects. It highlights the necessity of producing precise assembly and manipulation techniques in order to accomplish the intended goals [51].

14.4.5 Nanotechnology for actuation

A vital part of each device is its actuator, which enables movement and, more generally, interaction with the environment. Artificial molecular machines represent an intriguing approach to nano-actuation. The manufacturing of such structures must be predicated on chemical synthesis and manipulation techniques [52]. Remote stimuli, which include light, can produce and govern single molecules as well as supramolecular systems (such as creating isomerization). Moreover, they exhibit a number of drawbacks [53].

These consist of the following: (i) these are only available in solution and are difficult to handle separately; (ii) For continuous rotations or alternatively, motions without a mechanical coupling with a load, they are not very helpful; and (iii) an operation’s yield is often quite poor. A recent study emphasizes that structured molecular equipment assemblies, coupled with frameworks of metal and organic, are used as nanorobotic arms, in addition to outlining a roadmap (which excludes molecular switches due to their inability to generate useful work) [54].It also highlights the possibility of developing new kinds of enzyme-like mimics. These machines can exert forces well below 1 N, despite their promising size [55].

Other nanoscale actuators, often in tens of range of nanometers, are called biomotors. There has been some advancement in this sector since the initial attempts to use kinesin, a motor protein to create movement [56] and to bind to a surface F1-ATPase molecule in order to generate observable binding [57]. Nanoparticles have mostly been employed for nanoscale actuation [58]. Ten to fifteen years ago, CNTs were employed as main components that allowed actuation, demonstrating their potential [59, 60]. The performance of nanoparticles and nanocomposites is improving these days, particularly when combined with smart materials [61, 62].

Remote forces can also be used to guarantee actuators for nanoscale devices. When it pertains to magnetic fields, magnetized living things as well as nanoparticles with magnetic properties have been utilized, for example, magnetic resonance imaging [63]. Controlling the navigation of magnetic materials requires an understanding of their properties. Magnetic susceptibility (v), which is the ratio of the magnetic field applied (H) to the induced magnetization (M), is the crucial characteristic.

Micro-biorobots, also known as biohybrid microrobots, are devices that combine artificial and live components (such as cells or tissues), with the goal of small-scale exploitation of the living matter special properties within a combined system. According to this structure, the whole of living cells – for example, sperm or flagellated bacteria – are utilized to offer miniaturized robots their micro/nanoscale motility. They can be combined with magnetic nanoparticles, powders, or layers [64, 65], or used with bacterial cells that exhibit their own magnetic properties, which includes magnetotactic bacteria that are identified by organelles known as magnetosomes and constitute magnetic crystals [66, 67].

Although they have only been tested in vitro thus far, bio-hybrid inert microrobots derived from modified monocytes have been suggested [68]. To transport drugs to the right places, these microrobots must take advantage of monocytes’ chemotactic activity and transmigrating motility. Moreover, as chemotactic gradients may only be recognized at extremely short distances, using chemotaxis, a single targeting technique, would indicate and restrict treatment efficacy. This method would greatly expand its potential if it were linked to a proper “pre-navigation” of the microrobot by utilizing additional technical techniques, thereby permitting a closer approach to the target. Nanoparticles can play a significant role in this paradigm, for example, by acting as intracellular transducers to increase muscle contractility [69, 70]. To progress this research, a number of nanotechnological techniques will be required, particularly if complex biorobots made up of heterotypic cell clusters – multiple cell types – are to be studied [71]. Resonant devices, in which nanomechanical element is activated in one of its resonant modes, make up the majority of actuation-related nanoelectromechanical systems (NEMS) [72]. Interesting examples of NEMS for optomechanics have recently been published; including NEMS controlled by optical gradient forces [73] and NEMS that can regulate photonic crystal cavities’ optical biostability [74].

14.4.6 Nanotechnology for sensing

Technology for sensing is developing quickly. Since nanosensors would be tiny, ubiquitous, and undetectable, they are very intriguing. Above all, their sensitivity should surpass that of their macroscopic equivalents. At the moment, nanoparticles rule the nanosensor stage due to their many uses and operational mechanisms. By taking advantage of their altered conductivity upon exposure to particular compounds, nanotubes were first employed as sensors of the nanoscale [75, 76]. Presently, a number of nanoparticles are known to produce quantifiable results in response to specific response that is generated.

Gold nanoparticles are primarily used to detect chemical or biological targets by either modifying their surface to particular characteristic elements (such as antibodies, oligonucleotides, or reactant molecules) that release signals, which can be detected, like fluorescence, when they come in contact with the desired target or by taking advantage of changes in the nanoparticle’s conductivity, redox characteristics, or surface plasmon resonance character [77]. By utilizing their potential to function as catalysts and improve the transfer of electron, additional nanoparticles of metal (Ag and Pt), oxide nanoparticles (TiO2, SiO2, ZrO2, and MnO2), and semiconductor nanoparticles (CdS and PbS) may additionally serve as the basis for electrochemical sensors and biosensors.

Furthermore, as was previously mentioned for gold nanoparticles [78, 79], they can be functionalized by particular ligands.

One of the most ensuring nanoparticles to accomplish multifunctional sensing at the nanoscale is CNTs [80]. They can be utilized to transduce various physical inputs by taking advantage of diverse detecting techniques such as their special mechanical and electrical characteristics. Single-walled CNTs’ electromechanical characteristics are especially relevant for mechanical unit sensing. Covalent carbon–carbon bonds, for example, have a high degree of elasticity, making them suitable for use as nanoscale piezo resistors with gauge factors as high as 1,000 and the capacity to return to their starting state even after significant deformation.

Recently, polymeric nanoparticles have also been suggested. Polyacrylamide, poly(methyl methacrylate), poly(sodium styrene sulfonate), N-isopropylacrylamide, and other nondegradable and degradable materials are employed to create nanoparticles that are primarily used for chemical properties’ dynamic monitoring, cell and tissue metabolism, and response to external stimuli. Because of their high biocompatibility, they are particularly helpful in bio-related applications. Although their conformational variations in response to certain action can also be utilized, they are typically functionalized with target-specific ligands for this purpose [81, 82]. These days, flexible polymeric matrices containing piezoelectric nanoparticles, for example, barium titanate, zinc oxide, and alkaline niobate are being used to create nanocomposites. These devices transform mechanical energy into electrical outputs that may be sensed and stored using piezoelectric materials. They have primarily been proposed as energy harvesting systems [83, 84, 85]. This is an intriguing biorobotics application that enables the creation of gadgets that, when in use, can partially recharge their batteries. However, these devices are also appealing as force and stretching/bending sensors through nanoscale characteristics due to their capacity to react to both pressure and deformation stimuli.

Biological molecules have been recommended into nanosensors; the most promising ones are deoxyribonucleic acid and proteins (enzymes, antigens, and antibodies) [86, 87, 88]. When a binding event occurs, these molecules’ sensing mechanism is predicated on a conformational shift. For instance, the binding may cause an electrically active component and an electrode to move closer, enabling the detection of an electrical signal. Future integration of biological molecules with autonomous or semiautonomous miniature robots for cutting-edge medical treatments appears to have great potential. Nevertheless, there are currently no technologies for signal processing and collection that are as compressed as these sensor molecules [89].

14.5 Artificial intelligence in polymer science

In recent years, AI has grown as an essential platform to resolve scientific as well as technical issues in a range of fields. AI has enormous potential advantages, but it also poses significant risks and challenges. Scientific research will be more significantly and more rapidly impacted by this new trend. In order to comprehend the possible effects of AI, not only on their present activity but also on their fundamental mission as research and learning institutions, scientific institutions and universities everywhere urgently need to conduct strategic evaluations. This is crucial to maximize potential benefits and minimize potential drawbacks, as well as to make sure that new advancements are utilized to their fullest potential [90, 91].

AI is becoming a reality in daily life and is no longer merely a sci-fi “what might be” fantasy. This is a result of several recent discoveries and advancements that have been fueled in part by public and private funding as well as significant expenditures made by huge businesses. We are at the start of a new era that will profoundly alter many industries, particularly those where advancement has been impeded by the complexity of the data to be analyzed. Even though the scientific research industry is typically at the forefront of creating and utilizing new technology, it has demonstrated a startling lack of interest in the latest developments.

Our AI systems outperform the top human players at chess, go, and poker. These days, call center duties can be completed well by AIs without the callers realizing they are speaking to a machine. Currently, using a speech recognition program is less expensive than hiring a human assistant. The creation of systems that can enhance the capacity to solve complicated problems in a way similar to that of humans has demonstrated the validity of the Darwin challenge. The influence of these and similar discoveries on day-to-day operations has been minimal [92].

AI offers new opportunities for innovation by enabling data-driven forecasts, revealing hidden patterns, and automating time-consuming operations. However, several scientific disciplines, like polymer science, are not yet ready for its integration, and its rapid rise has proved disruptive. Adoption of AI has been particularly difficult due to the intricacies of polymer systems and the discipline’s predominantly empirical character. Many polymer scientists continue to encounter major obstacles, such as a lack of transdisciplinary training and technical complexity. Since they were discovered more than a century ago, polymers have mostly relied on trial-and-error testing. This is a time-consuming procedure that entails generating monomers, refining macromolecular structures, and modifying formulation characteristics in order to determine the optimal combination for a particular application. Even though the strategy has definitely led to important advances, it is still essentially gradual. Numerous options remain undiscovered because of the intricate and nonlinear interactions between structure and characteristics, as well as the enormous combinatorial explosion of polymer design possibilities. What innovative materials could be concealed in this vast, unexplored design space?

In such a huge and complicated world, how can we speed up the discovery of latest materials? No matter how ambitious, human ability cannot accomplish such a huge undertaking. Nonhuman intelligence, also referred to as AI [93, 94], enters the picture here, not as a solution but rather as a transformational tool, and aids that changes the way we conduct scientific study [95, 96, 97]. Artificial intelligence has already opened doors in disciplines like biology [98, 99]. For instance, Deep Mind’s Alpha Fold resolved a frequent protein folding problem [100]. This innovation demonstrates AI’s remarkable capacity to identify unidentified sequences and generate assumptions that outperform human perception.

Is polymer science the next area where AI will have a revolutionary impact? Imagine an artificial assistant who works round the clock to find solutions to urgent industrial and societal demands, evaluate enormous volumes of information to find opportunities that have been missed, and reveal important gaps in the literature. Working on the discoveries, a similar assistant may suggest a novel polymer that is precisely suited for a certain use, suggest an economical and effective production route, and take the polymer’s intended lifespan into consideration. Additionally, it might forecast how it will deteriorate and offer solutions to improve its sustainability and recyclability. However, this assistant wouldn’t merely provide theoretical recommendations. To carry out the suggested synthesis, it could easily communicate with an automated system. It may repeatedly optimize the process by evaluating real-time experimental data, and dynamically modifying response parameters to accomplish predetermined goals, while maintaining total safety. Practical concerns like locating and acquiring required solvents and reagents would also be taken care of, guaranteeing a seamless transition between expected and implementation. Additionally, this technology could consolidate, preserve, and structure information at each stage, producing thorough data that monitors development and offers valuable information to direct researchers. Although this may seem like a lofty goal for “today,” it is actually more realistic than we may realize. According to a recent study by Martin and colleagues describing “self-driving labs” of the future, the instruments required to enable seamless combination of AI, automation, and laboratory operations are either evolving or currently under development [101]. This vision is gradually becoming a reality due to rapid advances in robotics and AI. Perhaps, the scientists’ creativity and capacity to fully utilize this technology are the only real constraints. Another intelligent assistant might soon be available to aid with this duty as well. The number of published papers has increased, reflecting the exponential expansion of AI applications in polymer science in the last ten years. Though the AI’s ability in polymer science is clearly evident – many top-notch reviews have previously addressed this subject – the future is still unclear [102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107]. How does AI operate? Which resources should we acquire in order to start experimenting with and using AI in our studies?

14.6 AI as a novel paradigm in polymer science research

Fundamentally, AI is the machine’s capacity to mimic intelligence of humans, including pattern recognition, prediction, and data-driven learning [108, 109]. The word “AI” in chemistry frequently arouses interest but also perplexity, particularly in contrast to molecular simulations or physical modeling techniques. Polymer research has traditionally relied on conventional approaches, which include molecular dynamics and density functional theory simulations that use explicit equations a well as physical principles to determine changes such as phase transformations, chain conformations, or mechanical events.

14.6.1 Key machine learning techniques

ML is a branch of AI that focuses on creating models that can learn from data and produce conclusions or predictions without explicit programming [110, 111, 112]. ML is being used more and more in polymer science to assist material discovery, optimize synthesis [113, 114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119, 120, 121, 122, 123, 124, 125], and predict characteristics [126, 127, 128, 129, 130, 131, 132, 133].

ML is divided into three ways, as shown in Figure 14.2: supervised learning (SL), unsupervised learning (UL), and RL. The kinds of challenges these approaches tackle and the way these models learn from data vary [134, 135, 136, 137, 138, 139].

14.6.1.1 Supervised learning

Models in SL acquire knowledge using datasets with labels, in which every input has a corresponding output. This method is similar to conventional classroom instruction, in which a teacher guides students’ learning by giving them both accurate and inaccurate examples. In contrast to human learning, though, the development of model is assessed throughout training in order to modify its characteristics as well as boost corrections. Until the model achieves a high-performance threshold, which guarantees accurate predictions, the learning process is repeated iteratively.

Polymer research has embraced SL in order to use extensive experimental datasets to answer difficult material issues. Predicting the compatibility of polymers with solvents is one such use [140, 141].

Complex data analysis activities, especially those involving the processing of microscope images, have been automated with SL. The accurate localization and characterization of nanoparticles inside polymer matrices, which is typically accomplished by hand or with time-consuming image analysis techniques, is one of the primary challenges in polymer nanocomposite research. Qu et al. created a deep learning-based technique to identify and measure nanoparticles in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) pictures in order to solve this problem. They train a particular kind of neural network, CNNs, on labeled datasets of nanoparticle sizes and positions using an SL process [142]. An automated cropping and labeling technique (DOPAD) was used to extract 279,057 annotated subpictures from the 193 dataset, which comprises 72 TEM images.

When compared to manual approaches, the model greatly enhances the speed and accuracy of nanoparticle characterization by properly predicting the location and dimension of nanoparticles in newly formed TEM pictures. This method improves the study of polymer nanocomposite materials and makes it easier to conduct research on functional polymer-based nanotechnologies, advanced materials, and coatings.

14.6.1.2 Unsupervised learning

A powerful technique for identifying patterns in unlabeled data – that is, data without any predetermined outputs – is UL [143]. To uncover hidden correlations, clusters, or patterns, UL models autonomously analyze data, as opposed to SL, which depends upon certain input–output pairs. Stated differently, it is comparable to a student studying texts on their own to find recurring themes without the assistance of an instructor. As a result, UL is particularly helpful for interpreting complex polymer datasets where it may be challenging to identify or specify experimental labels. UL is specifically helpful in case of clustering, which groups polymers to similar structural or chemical characteristics together, and dimensionality reduction, which rectifies datasets of high-dimensional polymers through reserving important information [144, 145].

In polymer research, UL approaches have been effectively used to obtain insightful information from intricate datasets. Ziolek et al. [138] examined the micelles structure in nanoscale, made of linear block copolymers and four arms, using UL techniques. They found micelle structures groups with comparable corona arrangements by aggregating molecular conformations, and dimensionality reduction made the intricate structural changes easier to understand. Their approach allowed for a deeper comprehension of self-assembly mechanisms that are important for medications delivery and biomaterials creation.

14.6.1.3 Reinforcement learning

RL is an ML subset, which uses rewards for optimum behavior and interactions with the environment to teach models [146]. In contrast to SL, which trains models on datasets that are labeled, RL algorithms learn novel methods via trial and error. This is well-adopted for problems that call for sequential decision-making. Stated differently, it is like a toddler discovering that fire is dangerous only after coming in contact with it – the knowledge is acquired from actual experience rather than previous training.

Because RL entails long-term reward optimization, sequential decision-making, and exploration–exploitation trade-off, it is substantially more complex than supervised and UL. RL dynamically adapts methods based on ongoing input rather than learning from static datasets, necessitating sophisticated algorithms and substantial processing resources. Although these characteristics make RL an effective instrument for autonomous experimental control and improving polymerization processes, they also add to the complexity of its implementation and mathematics [147, 148]. Here are condensed examples to show how RL is used in polymer science.

With minimal real-world testing, Warren and associates [129] established an AI-driven closed-loop polymerization system that maximizes reversible-addition fragmentation chain transfer parameters to produce the required molecular weight and disparity. Their method incorporates concepts from RL, in which the system repeatedly tries reaction conditions, assesses the outcomes, and adjusts its strategy based on input from real-time analytical methods such as gel permeation chromatography and nuclear magnetic resonance. The system learns by engaging with the polymerization process rather than depending on preexisting datasets. It does this by methodically adjusting temperature and reaction time to maximize monomer conversion while minimizing disparity.

The main features of each ML strategy are compiled in Table 14.1 to offer a structured comparison, emphasizing the variations of information needs, analytical techniques, and applicability to research of polymer.

Table 14.1:Evaluation of approaches of key machine learning methods.

Characteristics Supervised learning (SL) Unsupervised learning (UL) Reinforcement learning (RL)
Category Labeled information (pairs of input–output) Unlabeled data No fixed classifications; develops by involvement
Aim Determine results (classification/regression) Reduce dimensions or organize related data into clusters Discover a series of steps to optimize rewards
Learning process Memorize from explicit examples Recognize hidden structures autonomously Learns by experience and input from the surroundings
Optimization focus Minimize loss (error) Identifies clusters, patterns, and representations Boost long-term benefits
Computational complexity Average Average–High Extremely high (complex decision-forming)

14.7 AI real-world tools

Platforms, cheminformatics tools, and programming libraries that can help researchers organize, analyze, and model polymer data are listed in Table 14.2. Open-source solutions that encourage openness, reproducibility, and accessibility in polymer research are especially beneficial since they enable a broader scientific community to participate in AI-driven materials discovery.

Python has become the preferred programming language for users who are just starting out with AI because of its ease of use, adaptability, and robust library ecosystem. User-friendly settings for writing and running Python code are offered by platforms like Jupyter Notebooks and Google Colab, which frequently do not require any installation or sophisticated computer power. These tools make it very easy for scientists for datasets loading, data cleaning, and preprocessing, deploying ML approaches. Open-source frameworks like Pandas and Numpy allow functional exploration along with large datasets alteration, including calculating averages, row filtering, and managing missing data.

Low-code or no-code platforms offer alternate points of entry for people who are afraid to start learning to code. Drag-and-drop interfaces for creating ML processes are provided by tools such as KNIME, which enable preparing data, training models, and assessing predictions, without requiring any code. Similar to this, Google’s Teachable Machine streamlines categorization procedures, and through user-friendly online interfaces, systems such as Azure ML and Google AutoML allow learning about custom models on available datasets.

Engaging in presentation of molecules along with utilizing cheminformatics tools such as RDKit, BigSMILES is one of the most potent uses of AI in polymer research. Researchers can transform chemical structures into machine-readable representations, including molecular fingerprints or SMILES strings, using RDKit, which can then be used as inputs for AI models [149]. Researchers may now represent structural changes and unpredictability in polymer chains because of BigSMILES, which expands the ability through offering stochastic polymers using standardized nomenclature. Scientists may easily predict properties like dielectric constants or biodegradability when associated along with particular databases such as Polymer Genome that provides pre-trained models for prediction of properties. Rapid hypothesis testing is made possible by the tools that Polymer Genome offers for investigating connections between molecular descriptors and polymer characteristics.

With AI technologies, navigating huge datasets – a frequent problem in data science – becomes much simpler. Consider, for example, a polymers dataset that includes their molecular weights, temperature stability, and mechanical properties. A researcher can use Python’s Pandas module to observe connections between molecular weight and tensile strength, compute averages for specific categories, and filter polymers with Tg over a predefined threshold in a fraction of time that it would take conventional tools such as Excel. In addition to saving time, these approaches create new opportunities for data analysis at a level that was previously unthinkable.

It is now a matter of when rather than if AI will be included into polymer research. The hurdles to entry have never been lower, thanks to the availability of open-source libraries, user-friendly platforms, and pre-trained models. Researchers can take their first steps into this revolutionary subject by beginning with basic tools like KNIME for drag-and-drop workflows or Scikit-learn for developing prediction models. There are a lot of thorough and useful resources accessible for people who want to use these technologies right away. Frequently, customers only need to download and execute pre-written code with little preparation [150, 151, 152, 153, 154, 155, 156].

14.8 Challenges and future directions in the convergence of AI and nanotechnology

The growing integration of AI and nanotechnology expresses variety of difficulties as well as generate novel possibilities for research. The key to this convergence is interdisciplinary cooperation, which brings together specialists from several disciplines, including computer science, materials science, and medication. Although it could be highly challenging, closing the knowledge gap across various fields is necessary for the effective creation of novel solutions. Large, high-quality datasets are essential for AI systems to flourish. Obtaining enough data can be an issue in many uses of nanotechnology. For reliable AI-driven solutions, it is essential to guarantee data accessibility, diversity, and accuracy.

The ethical implementation of AI in nanotechnology creates a number of ethical concerns, consisting of intellectual property rights, data privacy, and equitable access to AI-driven innovations. Accounting all these ethical issues is necessary to guaranteeing the responsible and equitable use of emerging technology as well as in building public trust. Rapid advancements in AI and nanotechnology are often difficult for regulatory frameworks to keep up with. Governments and international institutions must modify as well as enforce guidelines to preserve safety, security, and moral standards in these developing businesses. Scaling up AI-driven nanomanufacturing processes and nanodevices for practical applications could be challenging and expensive. It’s still difficult to achieve scalability without sacrificing accuracy and effectiveness. As AI and nanotechnology become more and more integrated into vital systems and applications, security and privacy issues become increasingly significant.

It is essential to mitigate security flaws and protect data privacy in order to stop abuse and online threats. The fusion of AI along with nanotechnology continues to influence science and technology in the future. Ethical norms, policies, and best practices for responsible usage of AI will be necessary for navigating the evolving world. Furthermore, new nanomaterials with specialized qualities will be made possible by AI-driven materials discovery, which will help a number of industries. AI and nanotechnology will make it possible to provide highly individualized healthcare on basis of patient’s unique genetic characteristics and medical requirements. Additionally, researchers will concentrate on energy-efficient AI-driven manufacturing techniques and green nanomaterial synthesis methods as well as other sustainable nanomanufacturing procedures. Complex simulations, optimization methods, and cryptography solutions will all be advanced by quantum computing, combined with AI algorithms. In the post-quantum computing age, this will ensure data security by opening the door for quantum-safe AI. Additionally, quantum materials development by AI improves quantum technologies such as quantum sensors and computation.

14.9 Data resources: accessibility, availability, and difficulties

Collaborative coding platforms and structured, high-quality datasets are essential for AI convergence in polymer research. Several initiatives have been developed to support scholars through giving repositories for exchanging curated datasets, machine-readable polymer representations, and ML models. These tools help scientists to promote creativity as well as discovery by effectively training and refining AI models. Several specific databases have been designed to allow the use of AI in polymer research through offering pre-trained models as well as structured data. BigSMILES provides standardized notation system for presenting stochastic polymers, Materials Project contains computationally derived polymer-related data, Polymer Genome provides AI-driven polymer property predictions, and NIST Polymer Database collects experimentally verified polymer properties and serves as benchmark for applications of AI.

Beyond databases that are polymer-specific, the polymer science community can take advantage of a number of general platforms that facilitate data accessibility, AI model sharing, and collaborative coding. These platforms not only make it easier to collaborate across disciplines, but they also provide ideas for creating customized alternatives that are exclusive to polymer research, increasing accessibility along with awareness. Zenodo is an open-access repository for ML models and structured datasets that provide proper attribution with digital object identifiers, while Hugging Face is well-known for collection of pre-trained AI models, which includes tools exclusive to polymers. GitHub is still a necessary platform for version-controlled AI workflows, collaborative development, and dataset storage, enhancing transparency and reproducibility. Even while these materials are becoming more widely available, there are still major obstacles to data accessibility and standardization. Much research continue to have uneven, fragmented, or unavailable datasets, either with little metadata or with important information about experimental results, characterization methods, and synthesis conditions. Polymer science runs the risk of falling behind fields like materials science and biology, where open data standards have already facilitated the rapid implementation of AI, in the absence of established data-sharing norms. To improve reproducibility and speed up development, funding organizations and scientific journals must actively promote change. They can do this by requiring the publication of structured datasets alongside research publications. Creating interoperable datasets that form the basis of AI-driven research requires developing community standards for collection of data, annotation, and distribution.

14.10 Future outlook

More than simply a technical breakthrough, the incorporation of ML with polymer science heralds the start of a revolutionary age. ML has the capability to entirely transform the design, synthesis, and optimization of polymers, changing both research and industrial uses. ML-driven techniques, ranging from autonomous testing to predictive modeling, are expected to speed up discovery while rendering previously unobtainable materials accessible.

14.10.1 Artificial learning’s growing application in polymer science

ML approaches will become more important in data-driven material discovery as polymer science experimental datasets continue to improve in size and complexity. Although SL has shown promise in forecasting important polymer characteristics, RL and autonomous learning will probably receive more attention in the future in order to support more independent and flexible research methodologies. It is anticipated that automated reaction optimization would benefit greatly from RL. RL allows an AI agent to interact with a polymerization process, continuously adjusting reaction parameters to maximize desired outcomes, in contrast to SL, which depends on historical data.

For instance, systems driven by RL could improve formulation procedures, speed up material discovery, and improve reaction conditions by continually gaining knowledge through real-time testing data. When combined with high-throughput experiments, the ML-based structures have the potential to investigate large chemical regions with previously unheard-of efficiency. The potential for UL for finding implicit structure-property correlations in polymer datasets has also been overlooked in polymer science. In polymer informatics, the absence of uniform labeling has been one of the main obstacles to its use, making SL techniques more instantly useful. But as structured polymer informatics frameworks develop further, autonomous learning will be an important tool for material design, latent pattern recognition, and molecular dataset clustering.

14.10.2 AI-powered experiments and self-selected labs

In the future of polymer science, which is anticipated to see the growth of AI-powered autonomous laboratories, standard synthesis, characterization, and optimization procedures will be managed by AI-guided robotic systems, greatly accelerating the research cycle. These self-operating labs will free up scientists to focus on more challenging scientific problems by transferring manual investigation to AI-assisted hypothesis-driven study. Through fusing AI to developed characterization methods and reaction monitoring systems, these labs will allow reactors that are self-optimizing to alter formulation parameters in real time and generate polymers through precise characteristics. Researchers will be able to effectively investigate novel polymer chemistries that are currently too difficult or resource-intensive to probe manually, thanks to the combination of AI, automation, and high-throughput testing. Real-time input from spectroscopy, chromatography, or other in situ monitoring methods could be used to continually improve reaction parameters in self-learning reactors. This strategy guarantees ideal material qualities while reducing trial-and-error testing. AI-powered formulation models have the potential to improve productivity and reproducibility in industrial settings by dynamically adjusting compositions of polymer for coatings, applications in biomedicine, and additive manufacturing.

14.10.3 Polymer science innovation and sustainability

ML is becoming more and more prominent as a crucial technique for creating ecologically friendly polymers due to the demand for sustainable materials. By forecasting integration in combinations of polymers and improving separation methods, ML models can revolutionize recycling operations, maximize the recyclability of polymer compositions, and assist in the design of biodegradable polymers with customized degradation profiles. ML-driven advancements in polymer science will be essential to achieving a circular economy by reducing energy requirements in reprocessing.

14.11 Conclusion

AI and nanotechnology are having a significant impact on the quantum computing field. AI helps to optimize quantum algorithms, but nanoscale components are crucial to the development of quantum processors. This convergence holds the potential to address challenging issues in domains like materials science and encryption and generate previously unparalleled computing resources. But with every technological development, there are issues that need to be resolved. To address the knowledge gaps between domain-specific scientists, nanotechnologists, and AI specialists, interdisciplinary cooperation is crucial. As this convergence develops, it is imperative to pay attention to legal usage of AI, data privacy, and scalability.

Future standards, suggested practices, and ethical principles ought to guide the proper use of AI in nanotechnology. Future developments in healthcare, environmental sustainability, and energy solutions will be greatly influenced by nanotechnology, while AI-driven materials research evolves to provide incredible discoveries. AI-powered quantum computing has the potential to completely transform a number of sectors. In summary, the combination of AI with nanotechnology seems to be evidence of human creativity and inventiveness. This convergence has the ability to change our world by addressing problems and moral dilemmas while pursuing state-of-the-art research as well as development. It can lead to new possibilities for knowledge and technological development and solve some of the most pressing issues of our day.

Editor’s biography

© 2026 Walter de Gruyter GmbH, Berlin/Boston, Genthiner Straße 13, 10785 Berlin 2026 Walter de Gruyter GmbH, Berlin/Boston, Genthiner Straße 13, 10785 Berlin

Dr. Rishabha Malviya completed his B.Pharm. from Uttar Pradesh Technical University and M.Pharm. (pharmaceutics) from Gautam Buddha Technical University, Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. His Ph.D. (pharmacy) work was in the area of novel formulation development techniques. He has 15 years of research experience and has been working as a professor in the Department of Pharmacy, School of Medical and Allied Sciences, Galgotias University, for past 12 years. His areas of interest include formulation optimization, nanoformulation, targeted drug delivery, localized drug delivery, andcharacterization of natural polymers as pharmaceutical excipients. He has authored more than 200 research/review papers for national/international reputed journals. He has 58 patents (19 grants, 38 published, and 1 filed) and publications in reputed national and international journals with a total of 350 cumulative impact factors. He has also received an Outstanding Reviewer Award from Elsevier. He has authored/edited/editing 58 books (Wiley, CRC Press/Taylor and Francis, Springer, River Publisher, IOP Publishing, and OMICS publication) and authored 150 book chapters. His name has been included in the World’s Top 2% Scientists list for the years 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024 by Elsevier BV and Stanford University. He is reviewer/editor/editorial board member of more than 50 national and international reputed journals.

Sonali Sundram completed her B.Pharm. and M.Pharm. (pharmacology) from AKTU, Lucknow. She has worked as a research scientist in the project of ICMR in King George’s Medical University, Lucknow. Then, she joined BBDNIIT and currently she is working in Galgotias University, Greater Noida. Her Ph.D. (pharmacy) work was in the area of neurodegeneration and nanoformulation. Her areas of interest include neurodegeneration, clinical research, and artificial intelligence. She has edited/authored/editing 32 books (Wiley-Scrivener Publishing, CRC Press/Taylor and Francis, IOP Publishing, Springer Nature,Apple Academic Press/Taylor and Francis Group, and River Publishers) and authored 45 book chapters. She has attended as well as organized more than 15 national and international seminars/conferences/workshops. She has more than eight patents, national and international, to her credit.

Dr. Sathvik Belagodu Sridhar is currently working as an associate dean and professor at RAK College of Pharmacy (RAKCOP), RAK Medical and Health Sciences University, Ras Al Khaimah, United Arab Emirates (UAE). He completed his Ph.D. in clinical pharmacy from Rajiv Gandhi University of Health Sciences, Bengaluru, India. He received an FIP fellowship for higher training in renal clinical pharmacy at Royal Adelaide Hospital and Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Adelaide, South Australia. He worked as an assistant professor and clinical pharmacist at JSS College of Pharmacy and JSS Medical College Hospital,Mysore, India, for 8 years and later joined International Medical University, Malaysia, as a senior lecturer in the Department of Pharmacy Practice from 2008 to 2010. He joined as an assistant professor in the Department of Clinical Pharmacy at RAKCOP, RAK Medical and Health Sciences University, in 2010 and worked as a professor and chairperson of the Department of Clinical Pharmacy and Pharmacology from 2018 to 2023. He has been honored with a prestigious teacher award by the Society of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (SPER). He has also received training in pharmacovigilance at the Uppsala Monitoring Centre, Uppsala, Sweden. He has 25 years of experience in teaching and practicing clinical pharmacy in India, Malaysia, and the UAE. His research interests include medication safety, pharmacovigilance, pharmacoepidemiology, and renal and psychiatry clinical pharmacy. He has more than 75 research papers published in reputed national and international journals, along with book chapters. He has presented more than 75 research papers at numerous national and international conferences and has been honored with many awards. He also serves as a reviewer for various national and international pharmacy practice-related journals.

Shivam Rajput has completed his B.Pharm. from Pt. B.D. Sharma University of Health Sciences, Rohtak, and M.Pharm. from Galgotias University, Greater Noida. He has authored/edited 10 books with Scrivener Publishing/Wiley/Apple Academic Press/Taylor and Francis Group, and Springer Nature. He has published more than 15 Scopus-indexed papers with reputed publishers such as Elsevier and Bentham Science. He has attended more than 10 international conferences.
